articles.body:
Tra le poche certezze legate al voto parlamentare tenutosi in Israele lo scorso 27 ottobre, c’è l’assenza di un vincitore netto: nessuna delle coalizioni principali ha infatti conquistato la maggioranza dei seggi. La coalizione del governo uscente guidata da Benjamin Netanyahu ha ottenuto 53 seggi, mentre il fronte dell’opposizione, guidato dall’ex generale dell’esercito Gadi Eisenkot, ne ha ottenuti 48. Entrambi gli schieramenti restano lontani dalla soglia necessaria (61 seggi) per formare un governo alla Knesset, il Parlamento israeliano da 120 deputati. Al fine di evitare un’altra tornata elettorale, il presidente Isaac Herzog ha invitato i due fronti principali ad approcciarsi all’attuale situazione di stallo «con la mente aperta». Uno dei risultati più inattesi delle elezioni è stato quello dei partiti arabi Ra’am e Lista Comune, che sono riusciti quasi a raddoppiare i propri seggi e far eleggere in totale 19 deputati. I loro voti permetterebbero all’opposizione di avere una maggioranza, anche se questa eventualità è complicata dal veto di alcuni partiti di opposizione.

In Italia sui social media il voto arabo-israeliano è stato raccontato da alcuni come un chiaro esempio del pluralismo della democrazia israeliana. Il deputato Luigi Marattin, noto per le sue posizioni pro-Israele, ha scritto su X il giorno delle elezioni: «oggi due milioni di arabi musulmani possono esercitare liberamente il loro diritto di voto, senza limitazioni alla libertà di stampa, senza restrizioni, e potendosi candidare direttamente per sedere nel parlamento  non stiamo parlando di nessun Paese arabo del Medio Oriente. Ma di Israele». Un mese fa, tuttavia, su petizione del partito di Netanyahu, il Likud, la Commissione elettorale aveva deciso di escludere i partiti arabi dalle elezioni, decisione poi annullata dall’Alta Corte di giustizia israeliana. A spoglio terminato, invece, il suprematista ebraico e Ministro della sicurezza nazionale, Itamar Ben-Gvir, ha chiesto l’arresto dei leader dei partiti arabi, accusandoli senza prove di frode elettorale.

I cittadini arabi israeliani rappresentano circa il 20 per cento della popolazione d’Israele: discendono da coloro che non abbandonarono le proprie case durante la Nakba (“catastrofe” in arabo), l’esodo forzato ed espulsione di oltre 700 mila palestinesi dai propri villaggi durante la fondazione dello stato di Israele nel 1948. Se in passato la comunità araba d’Israele aveva spesso boicottato le urne ritenendo inutile la partecipazione, in questa tornata il voto aveva un valore diverso. La nascita nel 2022 dell’esecutivo più a destra della storia del Paese e il conseguente aumento di retorica e violenze anti-arabe hanno spinto a una reazione democratica, favorita anche dalla mobilitazione dal basso di molte attiviste, decisive nel coinvolgere le donne e le comunità più periferiche. Il risultato è che nelle elezioni del 27 ottobre ha votato quasi l’80 per cento degli arabi israeliani aventi diritto.

La disinformazione anti-araba dell’estrema destra

Durante l’intera giornata elettorale Netanyahu ha presentato la mobilitazione degli elettori arabi come un rischio esistenziale, e per motivare i propri sostenitori ad andare alle urne ha definito la contesa una questione di «vita o morte». Secondo un’analisi condotta dai ricercatori e fact checker israeliani di FakeReporter, circa la metà dei contenuti pubblicati online e ricondivisi da Netanyahu durante il giorno del voto puntava ad alimentare la paura dell’affluenza araba. Per alimentare questa percezione d’allarme il premier israeliano uscente ha condiviso su X un video generato con l’intelligenza artificiale, in cui una persona raccoglie da terra delle chiavi attaccate a un portachiavi con la sagoma d’Israele e le consegna a Mansour Abbas, leader del partito arabo Ra’am. Nel video si legge: «Non diamogli le chiavi del Paese». Sempre sul proprio profilo, il primo ministro ha pubblicato immagini che pretendevano di documentare presunte code record ai seggi nelle località arabe, con lo scopo di allarmare i propri elettori. Le verifiche di BBC Verify hanno però accertato che almeno uno di questi scatti era un falso creato con l’intelligenza artificiale. Queste narrazioni sono state rapidamente riprese e amplificate dall’ecosistema mediatico di destra israeliano, tra questi l’emittente televisiva Channel 14, canale nazional-conservatore spesso definito la “Fox News israeliana”. Sempre FakeReporter ha rilevato che nel Paese la retorica anti-araba online tra il 27 e il 30 ottobre era aumentata del 428 per cento.

In seguito allo spoglio Netanyahu e i suoi alleati hanno rilanciato con insistenza la teoria delle “elezioni rubate”, sostenendo che la straordinaria affluenza della minoranza araba fosse pilotata da ingerenze straniere volte a islamizzare Israele. Nella diffusione dell’allarme ha avuto un ruolo anche David Zini, direttore del servizio di sicurezza interna Shin Bet e considerato politicamente vicino al premier, che ha accreditato l’ipotesi di gravi interferenze esterne tramite presunte risorse finanziarie destinate a incentivare la partecipazione elettorale araba e orientare i risultati delle urne. Tuttavia, a fronte dell’assenza di prove concrete, domenica 1° novembre il presidente della Commissione elettorale centrale, Noam Sohlberg, è intervenuto per sgombrare il campo dai dubbi, dichiarando che il voto si è svolto «in modo regolare e che i suoi risultati riflettono la volontà degli elettori». Sohlberg ha ribadito che, anche qualora i sospetti su finanziamenti esteri mirati a influenzare il voto dovessero trovare conferma, «questi non pregiudicherebbero l’integrità delle elezioni né il loro esito complessivo».

Nel frattempo sono stati scarcerati i due attivisti di Ra’am fermati dalla polizia nel sud del Paese il giorno delle elezioni con l’accusa di distribuire buste di denaro per corrompere gli elettori. Il quotidiano israeliano progressista Haaretz ha rivelato che il fermo era scaturito da una segnalazione diretta di Ido Norden, capo di gabinetto di Benjamin Netanyahu. Un alto funzionario delle forze dell’ordine ha confermato alla testata che «l’intero caso è nato all’interno dell’Ufficio del Primo Ministro», aggiungendo che la vicenda è stata strumentalizzata a fini politici e che non è emerso alcun elemento concreto a supporto delle accuse.

Il Qatar come grande manipolatore

Nel tentativo di delegittimare il voto, la destra israeliana di governo ha puntato il dito soprattutto contro il Qatar, accusandolo senza prove di aver manipolato le elezioni attraverso finanziamenti destinati a mobilitare l’elettorato arabo. Le accuse sono state prontamente respinte dal portavoce del Ministero degli esteri qatariota. Negli ultimi anni l’emirato è diventato agli occhi dell’establishment conservatore israeliano un bersaglio sistematico: rivale geopolitico accusato di sostenere Hamas e i suoi vertici, ma anche avversario mediatico per via dell’influenza del network mediatico Al Jazeera.

I tentativi di ritrarre il Qatar come una minaccia travalicano anche i confini nazionali. Un’approfondita inchiesta durata tre anni e diffusa recentemente, realizzata dai ricercatori Marc Owen Jones e Sohan Dsouza, ha recentemente documentato un network con chiare tracce riconducibili a operatori privati israeliani, protagonista di quella che gli autori hanno definito la «più grande campagna di sponsorizzate mai rilevata nell’UE». Attraverso centinaia di milioni di impression su Meta, TikTok e YouTube, l’operazione di disinformazione ha alimentato xenofobia e odio anti-arabo riadattando la teoria complottista della «Grande Sostituzione»: nei messaggi diffusi, il Qatar è stato dipinto come il nuovo finanziatore occulto dell’immigrazione di massa verso l’Occidente, prendendo di fatto il posto che la retorica dell’estrema destra assegna tradizionalmente al miliardario di origine ungherese George Soros. Questa campagna di disinformazione ha calibrato le attività a ridosso di appuntamenti sensibili: l’Italia sarebbe stata oggetto di questi contenuti sponsorizzati soprattutto in occasione delle Olimpiadi invernali di Milano Cortina 2026 e delle elezioni amministrative del 24 e 25 maggio 2026.

L’incognita sui prossimi giorni

La certificazione e la proclamazione ufficiale dei risultati elettorali israeliani sono previste per mercoledì 4 novembre, ma gli sviluppi politici restano un’incognita. In un atto che non avrebbe precedenti nella storia di Israele, Netanyahu starebbe valutando di non riconoscere l’esito elettorale, in uno scenario analogo alla campagna “Stop the Steal” promossa da Donald Trump dopo le presidenziali statunitensi del 2020 e basata su un teoria del complotto infondata secondo cui Biden sarebbe diventato presidente con frodi elettorali.

Quel che è certo è che il suo blocco politico sta inasprendo la retorica anti-araba e rendendo il clima incandescente. Il figlio del premier uscente Yair Netanyahu ha affermato che l’elettorato arabo israeliano rappresenterebbe «la più grande minaccia per la sopravvivenza dello Stato di Israele», seconda solo all’arsenale nucleare iraniano, per poi aggiungere: «il Paese non può sopravvivere quando il 20 per cento della sua popolazione si identifica con i suoi nemici e ne desidera la distruzione».

Non mancano le derive verso l’azione diretta: il deputato di estrema destra Yitzhak Kroizer ha esortato apertamente la cittadinanza a «uscire e armarsi», agitando lo spettro di una rivolta araba qualora i seggi conquistati da Ra’am e Lista Comune venissero annullati. Nel frattempo attivisti pro-Netanyahu si sono radunati sotto casa del leader dell’opposizione Gadi Eisenkot, chiamandolo traditore per via del suo tentativo di ottenere l’appoggio dei partiti arabi per formare un governo alternativo, e accusandolo di aver ucciso il suo stesso figlio. Eisenkot ha perso suo figlio Gal Meir Eisenkot nel dicembre 2023, mentre questo combatteva a Gaza con l’esercito israeliano. Sullo sfondo internazionale, intanto, Netanyahu starebbe spingendo per una nuova escalation militare contro l’Iran: una manovra strategica interpretata come un tentativo di far deragliare le trattative di Eisenkot.

articles.title: Delhi's toxic winter air is back - is the Indian capital prepared for pollution?
articles.summary: The Delhi government has announced a four-month winter action plan, but experts say that won't be enough.
articles.preview: There are two cardboard boxes in Meenu Rana's living room in Delhi. One is filled with Diwali decorations and twinkling lights. The other holds air purifiers. "The mornings have already started feeling stuffy. It will get worse in the coming days, so it's better to be prepared," says the 43-year-old teacher. She is not alone. Every year, as winter and the festive season approach, residents of India's capital begin preparing for something far less celebratory: months of breathing polluted air.
articles.body:
There are two cardboard boxes in Meenu Rana's living room in Delhi. One is filled with Diwali decorations and twinkling lights. The other holds air purifiers.

"The mornings have already started feeling stuffy. It will get worse in the coming days, so it's better to be prepared," says the 43-year-old teacher.

She is not alone. Every year, as winter and the festive season approach, residents of India's capital begin preparing for something far less celebratory: months of breathing polluted air.

Delhi and its satellite cities record some of the world's highest pollution levels through the year. But as winter sets in, the air often becomes unbearable.

Falling temperatures and slower winds trap pollutants close to the ground instead of allowing them to disperse. Smoke from crop residue burning in neighbouring states adds to emissions from vehicles and factories, as well as construction dust. Firecrackers used during festivals often worsen air quality.

The result is noxious air and a familiar question: why does pollution return year after year, and why hasn't more been done to tackle it?

This year, however, the Delhi government announced its Winter Action Plan months before the worst of the smog arrived. The plan is in place from 1 November to 28 February, covering the months when pollution usually spikes.

Experts have called this a step in the right direction, noting that in previous years measures were often rolled out only after the air quality got too bad to ignore. However, they say this by itself won't be enough, calling for more holistic, long-lasting measures.

Just days after the plan came into effect, the city is slipping back into a depressingly familiar pattern.

This week, a grey haze hangs over Delhi, along with a distinct smoky smell that residents unwillingly recognise. People complain of irritation in their eyes and difficulty breathing, and coughs and sneezes are heard everywhere.

For those who can afford them, air purifiers have become a household necessity. Outdoors, people wear masks or cover their faces with cloth, trying to protect themselves from the worst of the pollution.

Tackling pollution was among the promises made by the governing Bharatiya Janata Party during its election campaign last year. Its winter action plan is now a major test of that pledge.

The plan restricts the entry of older, more polluting vehicles registered outside Delhi and denies fuel to vehicles without a certificate which shows they meet emission standards. Demolitions and outdoor construction work that generate dust have been temporarily banned.

Private vehicle use is being discouraged - the government has asked offices to allow half of their employees to work from home, introduced staggered office timings for its staff and doubled parking charges. It says it will also strengthen pollution monitoring and enforcement and promote public transport and electric vehicles.

These measures are separate from the Graded Response Action Plan (Grap), which is overseen by the federal Commission for Air Quality Management.

Grap introduces restrictions in stages, with stricter measures kicking in as pollution levels rise. This week, its second stage is in force, restricting the use of diesel generators and burning of coal and firewood.

Expert say on paper, these actions collectively provide a roadmap for responding to rising pollution levels but their success ultimately depends on enforcement.

"There are a lot of positive changes as far as planning is concerned, but when it comes to execution, we probably still stand at the same level," says Parthaa Bosu, strategic adviser at the Environmental Defense Fund, a non-profit group focused on delivering climate solutions.

Others argue that the problem goes much deeper.

"If we want to reduce pollution, we need to set targets for every sector - including power generation, industry and transport - not just vehicle entry, construction and stubble burning," says Manoj Kumar, an analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air.

"We know how much each sector and each state contributes to pollution. We can set targets to reduce emissions from each of them over the next five years."

Bosu points out that an issue which does not get enough attention is secondary pollutants - when gases in the air react with sunlight, water vapour and other substances to form harmful particles that contribute to pollution.

"Pollution is not just caused by biomass burning or vehicles," he says. "Dust being stirred up from the ground, coal and fly ash, materials burned at brick kilns and the large-scale burning of urban waste are also contributing to the problem. And much of this is still not being stopped."

Delhi's pollution problem is also affected by what happens outside the city. Pollutants travel into Delhi from neighbouring states and other parts of northern India, worsening the situation, Bosu explains.

This means that measures taken by Delhi can achieve only so much. Tackling the problem requires neighbouring states and the wider northern region to work together, he adds.

In the meantime, pollution is harming people's health every day.

During winter, government monitoring stations in Delhi frequently record Air Quality Index (AQI) readings above 300, classified as "very poor".

On particularly bad days, readings can reach 500, the highest point on India's scale. That does not mean pollution cannot rise further, only that domestic trackers do not record it. International trackers such as Swiss-based IQAir have recorded readings close to 1,000 on some days.

The World Health Organization recommends average PM2.5 levels over 24 hours should not exceed 15 micrograms per cubic metre. In Delhi, levels are often at more than 25 times that limit during pollution season.

Dr Manoj Goel, pulmonology unit head at Fortis Memorial Research Institute near Delhi, says these tiny particles "can penetrate deep into the lungs and enter the bloodstream, triggering inflammation and affecting multiple organs".

Even short-term exposure can cause throat irritation, coughing, wheezing and breathlessness. It can also worsen existing heart and lung conditions.

A 2025 report, external by the Energy Policy Institute at the University of Chicago estimated that air pollution could reduce life expectancy in Delhi by up to 8.2 years.

For residents, the challenge is not just limited to breathing. The restrictions also disrupt everyday life.

Delhi is closely connected to its satellite towns, Noida and Gurugram, with thousands of people travelling between them every day for work. Long queues form at the city's borders as vehicles are stopped and checked, leaving commuters stuck in traffic for hours.

While the new rules offer some hope, frustration is growing.

Protests, political arguments and court interventions have become part of the annual cycle. But despite public pressure and government measures, the pollution returns every winter.

Rana keeps her windows closed and curtains drawn, and has added more indoor plants.

The arrival of another winter fills her family with dread, but unlike many others, they are not planning to move out of Delhi.

"I would have left the city long ago had there been an option, but my son has his school, my husband and I have our jobs as well, which makes it practically impossible," she says.

"What option do we have? It is unfair but we will have to live with it."

articles.title: Supermajority of Jewish Americans think Israel and Aipac drive antisemitism
articles.summary: Supermajority of Jewish Americans think Israel and Aipac drive antisemitism A supermajority of Jewish Americans think Israel and the American Israel Public Affairs Committee’s (Aipac) actions are increasing antisemitism in the US , according to a new poll. The poll commissioned by J Street, a US-based pro-Israel think tank, shows a deep gap between how Jewish American voters view organisations like Aipac and Israel’s occupation of the West Bank and Gaza Strip, compared to how the state of Israel and its allies in the US portray antisemitism. The poll says 66 percent of Jewish voters in the US believe that Aipac’s campaign spending against candidates who criticise Israel actually increases antisemitism in the country. articles.title: Turkey's parliament ratifies Mecca defence pact, clearing way for military support to Saudi Arabia
articles.summary: Turkey's parliament ratifies Mecca defence pact, clearing way for military support to Saudi Arabia Turkey's parliament on Thursday ratified the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, a defence pact between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey, clearing the way for Ankara to send military support to Riyadh amid attacks by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis against the kingdom. Under the agreement, signed by the three regional powers in August and sent to parliament for approval last month, an attack on one party constitutes an attack on all. A ruling party lawmaker told Reuters last month that Turkey would also submit a mandate to parliament allowing military personnel to be deployed to Saudi Arabia under the pact.

articles.title: Spain: Zelensky urges Latin America to help repair Ukraine's power grid
articles.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has appealed to Spain and Latin American countries for urgent help repairing Ukraine's damaged energy infrastructure. He also met King Felipe VI during the Ibero-American Summit in Madrid.
articles.preview: Speaking to Spanish, Portuguese and Latin American leaders, he appealed for transformers, power cables, generators and electronic equipment to restore infrastructure damaged by Russian attacks. Zelensky specifically identified Brazil, Mexico, Argentina and Colombia as potential suppliers of transformers, Chile for power cables and Spain for electrical equipment and generators. He stressed that Ukraine needed supplies compatible with its electricity grid and urged governments to establish direct contacts with manufacturers to accelerate deliveries.
articles.body: Speaking to Spanish, Portuguese and Latin American leaders, he appealed for transformers, power cables, generators and electronic equipment to restore infrastructure damaged by Russian attacks. Zelensky specifically identified Brazil, Mexico, Argentina and Colombia as potential suppliers of transformers, Chile for power cables and Spain for electrical equipment and generators. He stressed that Ukraine needed supplies compatible with its electricity grid and urged governments to establish direct contacts with manufacturers to accelerate deliveries. At the summit, Zelensky was seen speaking with UN Secretary-General António Guterres and attending talks alongside Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, Honduran President Nasry Asfura and other international leaders. The Ukrainian leader also met Spain's King Felipe VI at the Zarzuela Palace, where he was welcomed alongside Spanish Defence Minister Margarita Robles. His appeal placed Ukraine's energy needs at the centre of discussions, highlighting the importance of cooperation beyond Europe as Russian strikes continue to damage essential infrastructure. Zelensky emphasised that restoring the power network required not only international support but also rapid access to specialised equipment.

articles.title: The blame game: How the US midterm shock is shaping Israel’s race for PM
articles.summary: The Republican midterm rout is helping shape who leads Israel next, as Netanyahu’s US ties turn toxic.
articles.preview: The Republican midterm rout is helping shape who leads Israel next, as Netanyahu’s US ties turn toxic. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has long sold himself as the leader who will ensure that ties with the United States, the country’s most important ally, remain strong. The endorsement he received in the run-up to Israel’s parliamentary elections last month from US President Donald Trump added to that perception, in the same year as Washington and Tel Aviv jointly went to war against Iran.
articles.body:
The Republican midterm rout is helping shape who leads Israel next, as Netanyahu’s US ties turn toxic.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has long sold himself as the leader who will ensure that ties with the United States, the country’s most important ally, remain strong. The endorsement he received in the run-up to Israel’s parliamentary elections last month from US President Donald Trump added to that perception, in the same year as Washington and Tel Aviv jointly went to war against Iran.

Then came the US midterm elections, and the disastrous performance of Trump’s Republican Party. Early analysis of why the Republicans lost so badly has in part focused on that war with Iran, and the United States’s relationship with Israel. Both were highlighted by US Vice President JD Vance.

Suddenly, Netanyahu’s argument that he is the US-Israel relationship’s secret sauce looks much weaker. If anything, it can be argued that Netanyahu, and his policies – resulting in a genocidal war in Gaza, the Iran war, and numerous attacks in the wider region – have made Israel politically toxic in the US.

Many Israelis are now worried that the country can no longer rely on unquestioned support from the US. And as Israel’s political leaders jockey to try and form a government following the parliamentary elections, the opposition has laid the blame squarely at Netanyahu’s feet, and argued that it is another reason he should not be allowed to form the next government.

Yair Lapid, a former Israeli prime minister whose party is a member of the bloc seeking to unseat Netanyahu, stressed his own ties to members of the US Congress in a social media post. He added that he believed US voters were not so much against Israel as “against extremist ministers who say crazy things. They’re against settler violence; they’re against a government they don’t understand; they’re mainly against Netanyahu — for them, anything connected to him is toxic”.

Avigdor Lieberman, another opposition leader, echoed what many in Israel are said to suspect: that Trump’s election-day announcement that US military aid to Israel would end had been traded for his endorsement of the prime minister. “The price of Trump’s support for Netanyahu – $3.8bn dollars a year,” Lieberman wrote on social media.

“With America stopping the money it has channelled to Israel for so many years, the defence budget, already 7 percent of GDP, will have to rise. Israelis will feel it in their pocket. But then, you can’t be a rogue state and expect things to continue as before,” Ahron Bregman, an Israeli security analyst and senior teaching fellow at King’s College London, said. “In Israel, Netanyahu continues to do what he has always done so well, turning one segment of the population against the other. He’s now trying to delegitimise the Arabs by saying they stole the elections, in order to stop the opposition having the Arabs as partners.”

No substantial change

Israel’s general election on October 27 left Netanyahu’s right-wing bloc with 53 seats in parliament, eight short of the 61 needed to form a government.

The opposition bloc led by former army chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot got 48 seats, while the Arab-led parties – the United Arab List (Ra’am) and the Joint List – have 19 seats. The Arab-led parties have both said that they will support Eisenkot for prime minister.

Eisenkot and other opposition leaders have rejected suggestions of a unity government with Netanyahu, leaving him without a clear path to a majority.

It is now up to Israeli President Isaac Herzog to nominate a politician to form a government, but he has yet to do so.

As things stand, Eisenkot’s self-styled Zionist bloc, which has previously ruled out serving alongside the Arab-led parties, stands to benefit from their backing from outside the government, despite Netanyahu’s attacks.

Eisenkot’s prospects were boosted further on Thursday when United Torah Judaism (UTJ), Netanyahu’s longtime ultra-Orthodox ally, declined for the first time since 2009 to recommend him or anyone else to form a government, an apparent defection that weakens the prime minister’s position while giving a boost to his opponents.

But Eisenkot replacing Netanyahu as Israel’s prime minister does not necessarily mean that he will be able to reverse Israel’s declining popularity in the US. An April Pew Research Center poll suggested that public attitudes in the US are as negative towards Israel as they are towards Netanyahu, noted pollster Shibley Telhami, the director of the University of Maryland Critical Issues Poll.

“Our own poll found that most Americans would not change their view of Israel, even if there is a new government without Netanyahu,” said Telhami. “Any government of Israel would be swimming against the rising public tide … I don’t think any government of Israel could return relations back to where they were five years ago.”

articles.title: Who could be behind hoax bomb threats to European air travel?
articles.summary: There is no hard evidence so far linking airline bomb threats to Russia, Iran or any proxy groups.
articles.preview: The warnings came in thick and fast, targeting one airline or airport after another. In nearly all cases - London's Heathrow airport being a notable exception - they were taken to be credible enough to divert the aircraft in question, or even in Italy's case, to scramble fighter jets to escort it. They all turned out to be false, which does not, of course, mean that the next ones will not be real.
articles.body:
The warnings came in thick and fast, targeting one airline or airport after another.

In nearly all cases - London's Heathrow airport being a notable exception - they were taken to be credible enough to divert the aircraft in question, or even in Italy's case, to scramble fighter jets to escort it.

They all turned out to be false, which does not, of course, mean that the next ones will not be real.

It is hardly surprising that the simultaneous, co-ordinated nature of these airline hoaxes, coupled with other malicious actions across Europe, are causing some people to point the finger of suspicion at Russia.

Following a series of cyber-attacks and mysterious drone sightings over sensitive sites earlier this year, in the past few days we have seen the remote hacking of supermarket freezers, as well as a blood bank, a suspicious incident on Poland's border with Russia, and in August a drone attack Germany's Leipzig Halle airport which its interior minister publicly blamed on Moscow.

So is Russia behind this?

There are many who argue, based purely on circumstantial evidence, that this must surely be yet another example of "hybrid", "grey zone" or "sub-threshold" warfare - actions that damage a nation's infrastructure or society but which tend to be anonymous, deniable and which fall short of triggering Nato's Article 5 and thereby mobilising a response by the West.

Moscow is certainly furious with Nato for supporting Ukraine and, in doing so, frustrating the Kremlin's plans to swallow up that country and effectively terminate its independence.

Russian bloggers have also suggested that, if Ukraine's drones are currently making Russia's airports unsafe, and Western sanctions are blocking Russian airlines from European airspace, then why shouldn't Western nations feel the same pain?

But as of Thursday evening no hard evidence had emerged linking the airline hoaxes to Russia, Iran or any proxy groups controlled by them.

There is the email threat sent on Thursday morning to airport authorities in Rome, purporting to be from "Fighters of the Male State".

That name likely refers to the Russian group Muzhskoi Legion or "Male Legion", an ultra-right group with such extreme views it was banned by a Moscow court in 2021.

Yet, it retained tens of thousands of online followers on Telegram as it cheered on the full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine in the following year.

But the email sent to Rome, even if genuine - and who is to say it is not another group hiding behind that name? - is unlikely to provide the leads that police and airport authorities need to pin down who is generating these hoaxes and why.

For national police forces, airport authorities and transport ministries trying to work out who is behind these hoaxes and how best to mitigate their effect when they happen again, the task is not to go with who they think might be the most likely culprits but instead to follow the cold, hard leads - if they can find them.

articles.body:
US first lady hosts Russian, Ukrainian officials at the White House, urges two sides to build on recent local truce.

United States First Lady Melania Trump has urged Russia and Ukraine to build on a recent localised ceasefire and seek a more “enduring” peace, as she hosted officials from both countries at the White House.

Melania Trump spoke on Thursday at an event that the White House said is believed to be “the first time in American history that a First Lady has personally brought representatives of two nations at war to the White House for diplomacy”.

Those attending included Kirill Dmitriev, a special envoy of Russian President Vladimir Putin; Yana Lantratova, Russia’s human rights commissioner; David Arakhamia, leader of the Servant of the People party in Ukraine’s parliament; and Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine’s parliamentary human rights commissioner.

“Together, we can create something more enduring than a temporary ceasefire,” Mrs. Trump said, urging both sides to see the humanitarian truce in Oleshky “as a spark in a world of darkness”.

She said her role as “exclusive intermediary” was set out in written agreements signed by both countries, and that she was involved in every stage of the planning, including reviewing de-mining plans and evacuation routes.

Ukrainian representatives presented the US first lady with the Order of Princess Olga, first class, which President Volodymyr Zelenskyy awarded her earlier this week. She also gave the most senior officials present letters she had written to Putin and Zelenskyy.

The six-day truce covered the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky in Ukraine’s Kherson region and the surrounding area, and allowed aid deliveries and the evacuation of nearly 800 people.

An estimated 2,000 civilians had been left in the city. It was the longest multi-day truce between Russia and Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, and the first joint relief operation in four years and eight months.

The White House said Melania Trump mediated the truce, though Pope Leo XIV also pressed both sides to allow aid and evacuations, and that the two accounts of who brokered it have diverged.

The truce expired last Sunday with no extension, a day before a Russian bombing of an aid distribution point in Komyshuvakha, in the Zaporizhia region, killed at least 40 people, according to Ukrainian President Zelenskyy.

New US-brokered talks between Russia and Ukraine are expected to take place in Abu Dhabi on November 10 and 11.

articles.body:
Paraguay’s rightwing president, Santiago Peña, resigned on Thursday after a political and financial crisis collapsed the South American country’s banking system in recent days.

At the centre of the crisis is Ueno Bank, which in just a few years under Peña went from an obscure digital bank to one of the country’s largest lenders, claiming to have about 60% of Paraguay’s adult population as customers.

Last Monday, the central bank ordered Ueno into resolution over insolvency, freezing the deposits of 3 million customers, leaving hundreds of thousands of families without access to money for food and basic daily expenses. Bank executives were arrested, and people took to the streets in massive protests.

In power since August 2023 and with a term running until 2028, the 47-year-old economist was already facing impeachment proceedings that had broad support.

“Dear compatriots, today I address you at one of the most difficult moments of my life. With my heart set on Paraguay and with the conviction that our republic must always come before any person or circumstance, I have decided to submit my resignation as president of the republic,” said Peña in a video.

Ueno Bank began as a finance company in the 1970s and, in 2021, was bought by Grupo Vázquez, one of Paraguay’s largest business and industrial conglomerates. At the end of 2023, it received authorisation from the central bank, already under Peña’s administration, to operate as a digital bank.

The bank rapidly expanded its operations, attracting customers with generous cash-back offers on groceries and sponsoring Paraguay’s national football team. On Wednesday, the players released a letter “demanding” a “forceful response” from the government and the justice system.

The bank came to manage between $800m and $850m in deposits from state and pension entities, including retirement funds, prompting criticism over conflicts of interest because of Peña’s previous shareholding ties to Ueno Holding.

Peña said that, as an economist, he had merely made an “investment”, but that he had already disposed of all his shares. When the local press pointed to possible improper favouritism in directing state and pension funds to the bank, he called it a “false media campaign” aimed at weakening his government.

On Wednesday, opposition lawmakers and even members of Peña’s Colorado party filed an impeachment motion holding the president responsible for the collapse. He had been a shareholder in the group that ran the bank until early last year and, in recent months, had reportedly been ignoring warnings from the central bank and the media about its operations.

Political pressure intensified on Thursday morning when the ex-president Horacio Cartes, his former ally, posted a message endorsing the impeachment.

“We will not stand on the side of the theft of public, private and pensioners’ funds. We must think of the people and of the values we uphold in the Colorado party. We support the impeachment of the president of the republic, Santiago Peña, in order to restore the institutional order of the republic,” he wrote.

Other lawmakers followed suit and began debating impeachment when Peña released a video announcing his resignation.

“I do so thinking of the stability of our country, social peace and the need to preserve our democratic institutions,” said the now former president.

“I also want to apologise to the people if at any point I failed them … But today my priority is only one thing: the peace of mind of Paraguayans who trusted their savings to our financial system … My greatest wish is that the return of those funds is guaranteed,” he added.

Since the scandal broke, Peña has insisted in interviews and statements that he committed no wrongdoing.

Opposition senator Rafael Filizzola called the case “the biggest fraud carried out from political power in the democratic era … This is a bank created from political power, to use public money for private businesses linked to political power, with the president of the republic at the head of it,” he told 1020 AM radio.

Peña, a former finance minister who promised to rebuild a “great Paraguay”, was a key ally of the US president, Donald Trump, in the region – one of the few Latin American presidents to attend Trump’s second inauguration. US officials, including the secretary of state, Marco Rubio, repeatedly praised him as a “strategic partner”, and Peña recently flew to Washington to discuss critical minerals and economic cooperation. Neither Rubio nor Trump has yet commented on Peña’s resignation.

It is still unclear who will replace him or when, because his resignation must, in theory, be accepted by Congress – in which case the vice-president, Pedro Alliana, would take over. Alliana is also suspected of involvement in the Ueno Bank scandal, which he has denied.

About an hour after Peña’s announcement, the lower house unanimously approved the impeachment motion, which now goes to the senate. If approved, even after his resignation, he would lose his senate seat and, with it, parliamentary immunity, leaving him to face any criminal proceedings in the ordinary courts.

articles.title: Sánchez defiende la diversidad ideológica en la Cumbre Iberoamericana: “Creemos en el valor de este foro multilateral”
articles.summary: El presidente del Gobierno destaca la adopción de una declaración conjunta que logra reflejar un “mínimo común denominador” entre los 22 países
articles.preview: El presidente del Gobierno destaca la adopción de una declaración conjunta que logra reflejar un “mínimo común denominador” entre los 22 países El presidente del Gobierno, Pedro Sánchez, ha hecho una defensa férrea de las cumbres iberoamericanas y de su valor como espacio de diálogo en un mundo convulso. “Creemos en el valor de este foro multilateral”, ha expresado este jueves al término de la cita en Madrid.
articles.body:
El presidente del Gobierno destaca la adopción de una declaración conjunta que logra reflejar un “mínimo común denominador” entre los 22 países

El presidente del Gobierno, Pedro Sánchez, ha hecho una defensa férrea de las cumbres iberoamericanas y de su valor como espacio de diálogo en un mundo convulso. “Creemos en el valor de este foro multilateral”, ha expresado este jueves al término de la cita en Madrid.

En una comparecencia junto al secretario general iberoamericano, Andrés Allamand, y Nasry Juan Asfura, presidente de Honduras, país que recibe de España la presidencia pro tempore de la organización, Sánchez ha defendido el éxito de esta XXX edición, tras haber tocado fondo en la anterior cumbre en Ecuador (2024). “España de nuevo siempre da lo mejor de sí en este tipo de eventos internacionales”, ha expresado.

El presidente ha ensalzado el logro de resultados concretos, como la puesta en marcha de una red de reducción de los desastres naturales, la alianza para la inteligencia artificial, la carta de movilidad académica (una especie de embrión de Erasmus iberoamericano) y otra de cuidados, que trata de situar este sector en el centro de las políticas públicas de la región. “Estamos hablando de acuerdos sustantivos que reflejan lo que somos: una comunidad [...] de valores compartidos”, ha resaltado.

El jefe del Ejecutivo ha reconocido la heterogeneidad de una organización con 22 países: “Por encima de las diferencias ideológicas que tenemos, lógicamente, porque somos una comunidad diversa, también desde el punto de vista ideológico, y de las legítimas diferencias que se puedan tener entre naciones, creo que a nuestra comunidad le mueve la voluntad de construir un mundo mejor”.

En la sesión plenaria, celebrada a lo largo de la mañana en la galería de Colecciones Reales, junto al Palacio Real, las delegaciones han logrado también dar el visto bueno a una declaración conjunta, un hito considerable si se tiene en cuenta que las fracturas entre países provocaron que en 2024 se cerrara la cumbre sin texto común por primera vez desde la primera cita en 1991. Es cierto que ha sido en esta ocasión un comunicado de mínimos, que ha requerido trabajo de orfebrería para lograr el consenso y que, por ejemplo, condena el bloqueo estadounidense a Cuba, aunque sin citar al país caribeño expresamente. Además, hasta cuatro países (Argentina, Colombia, Costa Rica y Paraguay) se han “disociado” de este párrafo concreto. Pero ha recibido luz verde.

“Es una declaración que refleja la diversidad de opiniones y de posicionamientos que tiene hoy el sistema iberoamericano”, ha dicho Sánchez sobre unas divergencias que no son nuevas. “Siempre ha habido un esfuerzo por tratar de encontrar ese mínimo común denominador y en este caso se ha logrado y creo que es el resultado óptimo”. Sobre el voto de disenso a la postura general sobre Cuba, Allamand ha agregado: “Es absolutamente normal que, existiendo consenso respecto del núcleo fundamental de la declaración, algunos países quieran expresar un punto de vista particular”.

Sánchez también ha restado importancia a las ausencias de líderes de máximo nivel como Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, recién reelegido para otro mandato de cuatro años en Brasil, y la presidenta mexicana Claudia Sheinbaum, los dos países más grandes y con las principales economías de Latinoamérica, además de bastiones de la izquierda y aliados de Sánchez.

No ha entrado a valorar los motivos de su ausencia. “Todos los países han estado representados”, ha afirmado en cambio. “Y me gustaría en primer lugar agradecer de corazón, porque sé que todos tenemos agendas muy difíciles, muy intensas, que la política doméstica, pues al final es la principal tarea que tiene todo gobernante, el esfuerzo de tomar un avión, de venir a Madrid”, ha dicho en referencia a quienes sí han viajado.

Allamand también ha incidido en la importancia de un foro como el iberoamericano en tiempos de fracturas globales. “Esta cumbre se efectúa en un momento de un orden mundial convulso, en reconfiguración, lleno de incertidumbre, pero donde hay un embate muy firme al multilateralismo”, ha asegurado. Esta cumbre, ha insistido, reafirma la importancia de esa diversidad de visiones. “Que haya aquí 22 países, que esté aquí el secretario general de Naciones Unidas [António Guterres], el presidente del Consejo Europeo [António Costa] y que se reafirme este concepto de que el multilateralismo sí funciona [...] es muy importante”. Y ha asegurado que la comunidad tiene muy buenas expectativas de futuro tras lo que ha llamado “la cumbre de la reafirmación”.

En la comparecencia, Sánchez también se ha visto obligado a responder, de manera inevitable, sobre su cara a cara, y el brevísimo apretón de manos, con el presidente argentino, Javier Milei. Ha sido uno de los focos de la cumbre. Ambos se veían después de un historial de choques, y tras la ristra de insultos que le lanzó el argentino durante su reciente visita a España, hace solo dos semanas. Durante su intervención en el plenario, Milei ha homologado el socialismo con el fascismo, pero ha esquivado un nuevo ataque personal contra Sánchez.

El presidente español le ha agradecido a su homólogo argentino su participación y asistencia, y ha agregado: “Los presidentes estamos para unir, especialmente cuando estamos en cumbres internacionales [...] El insulto no forma parte de mi forma de entender y hacer política”.

articles.body:
Gadi Eisenkot, the main rival to Benjamin Netanyahu, secured endorsements on Thursday from a majority of lawmakers to try to form a government but Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, said it was still unclear who could break the deadlock and that he would decide on Sunday which of the two men should try first.

Of the Knesset’s 120 elected lawmakers, 67 had endorsed Eisenkot through several days of talks with Herzog, while 46 endorsed Netanyahu. Herzog said on Thursday that while the “results of the consultations may appear clear”, there were “mutual vetoes between the blocs and within the blocs themselves” that make it difficult to say who has the best shot to form a government.

He said he would make a pick on Sunday, and that he would hold “personal talks with some of the party leaders” over the Israeli weekend, which runs Friday-Saturday.

A bitterly contested election last month, seen by many observers as one of the most consequential for Israel in many decades, ended with neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot, a former military general and chief of staff, securing a clear pathway to power.

Netanyahu’s coalition lost its majority, dropping from 68 to 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset. The Change bloc of Zionist parties led by Eisenkot has 48 seats, leaving parties representing Israeli Palestinians as potential kingmakers with a record 19 seats. The Joint List has 11, while the more conservative, Islamist Ra’am has eight.

In Israel’s political system, the otherwise largely ceremonial president decides which candidate has the best initial chance of building a stable coalition to rule.

Both Arab-majority parties reported backing Eisenkot, according to Haaretz. United Torah Judaism, though often aligned with Netanyahu, did not endorse either man.

Turnout among Arab Israelis – Palestinians with Israeli citizenship, who constitute 20% of the population – more than doubled to about 80%, transforming the political landscape. Palestinians in the occupied West Bank and Gaza had no vote.

The leader of Israel’s main Palestinian coalition has admitted to “disagreements with Eisenkot on many issues” but said on Thursday that Palestinian voters wanted change after facing intensified racism, discrimination, crime and exclusion under the current coalition.

“We are not choosing between good and better but between what we see as bad and even worse,” Yousef Jabareen said, according to Israeli media.

Last month, Jabareen told the Guardian that the first demand of Arab Israeli voters was to get rid of the Netanyahu government, and in particular its most extreme members, Itamar Ben-Gvir, the national security minister, and Bezalel Smotrich, the finance minister.

Eisenkot has also put conditions on any potential coalition with Arab parties: they have to recognise that Israel is a Jewish state, accept compulsory national service – either civil or military – and denounce Hamas as a terrorist organisation.

Jabareen and the Joint List have suggested they would support an opposition from the outside with tactical voting in the Knesset. Ra’am has said it would join a new government led by Eisenkot.

Herzog, who met delegations from the Palestinian Israeli parties and other small parties, has called on all to help avert another round of elections.

“Any reasonable person need only look at the security and diplomatic challenges before us, at the changing region around us, and remember the issues tearing us apart from within, to understand that an immense responsibility rests upon us,” Herzog said.

Netanyahu remains prime minister in a caretaker government until a new coalition is formed or there is another election, which must be held if no candidate succeeds.

Though the 77-year-old political veteran did better than expected in the vote and his Likud party won the most seats, his nationalist-religious coalition, the most rightwing government in Israel’s history, lost its governing majority.

Netanyahu, at risk of losing power, has seized on an investigation by election officials into possible vote tampering to cast doubt on the results, accusing Israeli Palestinian-led parties of stealing the vote. Critics accuse Netanyahu and his partners of trying to undermine the results, which he denies.

Israel’s Central Election Committee said on Wednesday that the election’s integrity had not been compromised. The head of the committee, the supreme court justice Noam Sohlberg, has called on the country’s elected officials to protect public trust.

“This is a real danger. One of the foundations of democracy is the peaceful transfer of power,” Sohlberg told Herzog at his residence on Wednesday. He said high voter turnout, including among the Arab minority, was a blessing.

Netanyahu’s allies on the far right, including Ben-Gvir, have called for the immediate arrest and interrogation of Arab party leaders.

articles.body:
The Duchess of Sussex’s estranged half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr, has been named as a “person of interest” in the Philippine authorities’ inquiry into child sexual abuse image allegations made against her father, Thomas Markle Sr.

The country’s interior and local government secretary, Jonvic Remulla, told a press conference in Manila there were “signs that point that the son is involved in the crime as well”.

He added that Markle Jr, 60, who alerted local police and the FBI to images he found in his father’s belongings, was not yet being treated as a suspect. His alleged involvement is not thought to be directly linked to the material he handed to the police.

More than 7,000 photos and one video – all of under-age males and females of Asian, Latin and European descent, with some as young as 10 and 11 – were uncovered, Remulla said.

He described the images as “the most deplorable displays of impunity towards sexual activity that I have ever seen”.

Markle Sr, 82, who is estranged from Meghan, has reportedly been moved into a care home for dementia patients in the US where he is now living.

Remulla said: “We’re determining if [the] son is involved … There are signs that point that the son is involved in the crime as well but only as a person of interest so far.”

He added: “We will know in the next few days.”

Markle Sr, who returned to the US from the Philippines in May, has admitted paying for sex in the Philippines but he has strongly denied possessing child abuse imagery, and suggested he had been “set up”. His son remains in Cebu City in the Philippines.

Remulla has previously described Markle Sr as “a possible sex offender of the grossest kind”.

Markle Jr reported his father after claiming to have found four storage boxes at his father’s home in the Philippines containing “hundreds, if not thousands” of child sex abuse images.

Police and FBI agents have since been investigating whether Markle Sr was in possession of any illegal images while living in the Philippines and in Mexico, where he previously lived, and where other illegal images were reportedly found in one of his storage units.

Markle Jr was recently interviewed at his home in Cordova, Cebu, as part of an international, multi-agency meeting via Microsoft Teams, according to the Sun, which first published the claims. He gave his statement to an FBI agent based in Florida, who specialises in child sex abuse cases.

In a statement issued when the allegations against her father were first published, Meghan said she was “deeply distressed” by the claims. She said she had been informed of disturbing allegations against her father in 2018 and had kept him from having contact with her children, Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five, to protect them.

articles.title: Arrests and investigations as Serbia begins post-election clean-up
articles.summary: The landslide victory of the Students' List in Serbia's general election seems to have removed a blockage in the justice system: Cases that were long stalled are now suddenly moving forward.
articles.preview: November 5, 2026 The landslide victory of the Students' List in Serbia's general election seems to have removed a blockage in the justice system: Cases that were long stalled are now suddenly moving forward. Air Serbia flight JU134 from Belgrade to Moscow on November 3 was already deep in Lithuanian airspace when the crew received instructions to return to the Serbian capital.
articles.body:
November 5, 2026

The landslide victory of the Students' List in Serbia's general election seems to have removed a blockage in the justice system: Cases that were long stalled are now suddenly moving forward.

Air Serbia flight JU134 from Belgrade to Moscow on November 3 was already deep in Lithuanian airspace when the crew received instructions to return to the Serbian capital.

Among the passengers were three senior figures from the regime of former President Aleksandar Vucic: Aleksandar Vulin, former defense and interior minister and former head of Serbia's Security Intelligence Agency (BIA), Dusan Bajatovic, long-serving director of state-owned gas company Srbijagas, and Nenad Popovic, a minister without portfolio.

All three are well known in Serbia for their close ties to Moscow and for controversies, including allegations of corruption and abuse of public office.

According to unofficial reports published by several media outlets, the plane was ordered back because of a security breach: Vulin had allegedly boarded without undergoing the mandatory security screening.

Since 2023, Vulin has been under US sanctions over what Washington described as "engaging in corrupt and destabilizing activities that undermine the rule of law in the Western Balkans."

Unusual episode

Vulin told the media that he was travelling to Moscow to discuss extending a gas agreement with Russia.

Bajatovic, however, said he did not know why Vulin and Popovic were travelling to Moscow and denied that the two would attend the scheduled meetings on gas supplies.

The incident might have remained nothing more than an unusual news item had it not occurred at a time when Serbia is undergoing a major political transformation.

Judicial developments unfold at remarkable speed

Just nine days earlier, on October 25, the student-backed list won a landslide victory over the Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) in the parliamentary election, ending 14 years of political dominance by Aleksandar Vucic and the SNS, who maintained close relations with Moscow.

Although the new majority has yet to take control of any levers of power, the days after the election brought a series of developments that would have seemed unimaginable just a few weeks ago.

Arrests, new criminal proceedings and the reopening of previously unresolved cases began to unfold at remarkable speed. Some of these cases strike at the very foundations of the system built during the SNS years in power.

"This paints a sad picture of the Serbian prosecution service," prosecutor Bojana Savovic told DW.

Savovic sees the sudden action on the part of prosecutors as an attempt to ingratiate themselves with the new authorities.

"With these actions, they are showing what they could have done but were unwilling to do until just ten days ago," she told DW. "I hope this speed of action will not come at the expense of the quality of indictments and that these are not personal vendettas within the old regime."

Allegations of vote-buying and high-level corruption

Prosecutors have also launched a series of investigations into suspected electoral manipulation, corruption and abuse of public office.

Four people were arrested on suspicion of vote-buying in Novi Sad. Six others were detained in Mali Zvornik on suspicion of helping citizens from Bosnia and Herzegovina register their residence in Serbia so they could vote.

One of the most high-profile cases is the arrest of Davor Macura, the owner of Alta Bank, who is suspected of illegally accessing the bank's vault and removing the equivalent of about €383 million ($430 million).

His arrest came just days after the National Bank of Serbia revoked Alta Bank's license and initiated bankruptcy proceedings. Macura has been publicly associated with the SNS, while his bank had significant business dealings with the state and a large number of Russian clients.

Senior police officials, the head of the Republic Hydrometeorological Institute and several managers of public companies have also been arrested over suspected abuses of office and rigged public procurement procedures.

Alleged destruction of documents

Students and representatives of the new political majority are demanding investigations into corruption cases that have remained unresolved for years.

Their message is that no one should be above the law and that prosecutors and courts must do their jobs — or be held accountable for failing to act.

"When you want the rule of law and when you want something to be done, it is possible. Our regulations allow for it. But it was obvious that there were people obstructing the entire system, putting cases in drawers and leaving them unresolved," Tanja Arsic, an incoming MP from the Students' List, told DW.

In the days after the election, however, reports and video footage emerged that suggested official documents may have been removed or destroyed in state institutions and public companies.

On October 29, Prosecutor General Zagorka Dolovac responded by issuing a binding instruction to all chief public prosecutors to prevent the destruction of official and other records.

The Students' List also called on employees in state institutions and the media to report any destruction of documents to prevent what they called abuse by the outgoing authorities during the transition of power.

Savovic points out that even an attempt to destroy official records is punishable by law.

How high up will investigations reach?

But will the institutions really investigate those who were once at the very top of Serbia's political power structures?

Former President Aleksandar Vucic said he is not afraid of being arrested and that no evidence of financial wrongdoing will be found against him.

"I don't sign or do anything when it comes to money, and nothing can be found in that regard," he said.

But accountability is not just about who signed a document. It is also about establishing who made the decisions, who gave the orders and who wielded the real power to influence the deals now under investigation.

"It would be tragic if the biggest players, whose arrests are expected, were prosecuted without sufficient evidence. Or if they were charged with something far less serious than what they actually did," said Tanja Arsic.

The real test is yet to come

Bojana Savovic makes a point of saying that ultimately, the success of the prosecution service won't be measured by the number of politically popular or populist arrests that are made, but by final convictions and the permanent confiscation of assets acquired through crime.

Arsic agrees and warns that conducting high-quality investigations and gathering robust evidence must take precedence over speed.

"The prosecution must not bring indictments if there is not enough evidence. That would be disastrous," she said. "If things are rushed just to achieve a result, only for the cases to end in acquittals because the prosecution failed to prove the charges against people who were at the top of the government — that would be even more disastrous."

But will that be possible within the existing structures? Savovic is not convinced that it will.

"For decades, people whose only qualification was blind obedience, reading the political climate and self-censorship were promoted in the prosecution service and the courts. Without fundamental changes in the judiciary, the police and the security structures, I see no possibility of a substantial and lasting transformation of society," she said.

The real test will come in the courtroom. The verdicts in these cases will show whether Serbia is finally breaking with its old system of power or merely replacing one set of power brokers with another.

articles.body:
Commonwealth

Commonwealth leaders meeting in Antigua and Barbuda on Wednesday have welcomed Britain’s agreement to join talks on the legacy of the transatlantic slave trade. Britain's pivotal role in slavery has long strained relations with its former colonies.

A joint communique issued at the end of the summit, set out the details.

"Our heads welcome the agreement of the government of the United Kingdom to engage in a structured, time-bound, inclusive, and good faith dialogue with affected parties addressing the transatlantic trafficking of enslaved Africans and its historical harms," Commonwealth Secretary-General Shirley Botchwey told the summit.

Gaston Browne, Prime Minister of Antigua and Barbuda, said the talks are expected to take place within the next 12 months:

"We have also agreed in principle that by the end of this year, or early next year, that the whole framework for the dialogue will be established. And again, we are not going to make any unreasonable demands on the United Kingdom but it's a matter that has to be addressed and to be addressed in a mature way, and he [the UK Prime Minister] understands that, and his full cooperation."

In an address to the summit on Tuesday, Britain's King Charles III said slavery was a "shameful chapter of history" but stopped short of apologising.

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he wants to bring a “new approach” to the discussion and opened the door to issuing a formal apology on behalf of the British state. However, UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has ruled out the possibility of financial reparations.

"It's not the right answer," Miliband said in an interview on Wednesday. "It's not practical. It's not feasible for us, but there are things we can work on co-operatively."

At the summit in Antigua and Barbuda, Burnham floated the idea of a "debt reset" plan for the poorest Commonwealth countries that could alter interest rates on repayments.

"I've been very clear that we do not support reparations," Burnham told reporters on Tuesday, "but it's not the case that we don't support countries in the Commonwealth around development helping them with debt issues that they've got."

articles.body:
Nuclear weapons

These experts have gathered in the Namibian desert to find out whether a nuclear weapons test has been done there.

The Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty (CTBT) prohibits all nuclear weapons test explosions.

Although it is yet to enter into force, a global norm against nuclear testing is emerging.

“This is only the third exercise, Integrated Field Exercise, in the 30 years history of the Organization. It is the first big exercise conducted on the African continent,” said Oleg Rozhkov, Director of On-site Inspection Division, CTBTO.

The CTBTO's on-site inspection (OSI) system is designed to establish the facts and ascertain whether a nuclear weapons test explosion has been conducted.

The field exercise hosted by Namibia will prove whether that capability can deliver when it is needed.

More than 2.000 nuclear tests were carried out before the Treaty opened for signature in 1996; fewer than a dozen have been conducted since.

“It’s absolutely amazing that 188 countries out of the possible 196 in the world have signed on to the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty. That means that every one of them has agreed to the object and purpose of the Treaty that is no further nuclear tests," said Dr Robert Floyd, executive secretary of the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty Organization (CTBTO).

The exercise which has brought together 250 experts runs until 20 November. It is the third of its kind, following earlier exercises in Kazakhstan in 2008 and Jordan in 2014.

articles.title: Saudi coalition intercepts missile fired towards Medina
articles.summary: Interception comes after Saudi civil defence agency warned of potential danger near the strategic port of Yanbu.
articles.preview: Interception comes after Saudi civil defence agency warned of potential danger near the strategic port of Yanbu. The Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen’s Houthis has said it intercepted a ballistic missile fired by the Iran-aligned armed group towards the Medina region, home to one of Islam’s holiest cities. The announcement on Thursday came just minutes after Saudi Arabia’s civil defence agency warned of potential danger in the area near the strategic port of Yanbu.
articles.body:
Interception comes after Saudi civil defence agency warned of potential danger near the strategic port of Yanbu.

The Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen’s Houthis has said it intercepted a ballistic missile fired by the Iran-aligned armed group towards the Medina region, home to one of Islam’s holiest cities.

The announcement on Thursday came just minutes after Saudi Arabia’s civil defence agency warned of potential danger in the area near the strategic port of Yanbu.

“Air defence intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the terrorist Houthi militia toward the Medina region,” coalition spokesman Turki al-Malki said in a post on X.

The Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), have rejected any suggestion they were targeting the city, saying such accusations were a “blatant and grave falsehood”.

Houthi Military spokesman Yahya Saree wrote on X that “our operations target only oil facilities and military bases” and called the allegation a lie.

Among their attacks on airports, energy infrastructure and military sites, the Houthis have targeted the port of Yanbu on several occasions in recent months.

“A warning has been issued by the National Early Warning Platform in Yanbu Governorate to alert of a potential danger,” read a statement published by the agency online.

The agency later announced that the threat had passed.

Yanbu is a major oil export hub and a key outlet for oil shipments transported through the kingdom’s East-West pipeline.

The port and pipeline have played a key role since the outbreak of the United States-Israeli war on Iran in February, helping Riyadh ship crude and fuel to global markets.

Separately, Yemen’s internationally recognised government forces made gains in the Sanamat area in Taiz governorate, where fighting continues to rage.

Colonel Majed Abdullah al-Nazili said on Thursday that government forces carried out 1,298 “targeting operations” against the Houthis in the past 24 hours and “managed to gain control” of Sanamat.

The latest operations killed about 400 Houthi fighters and destroyed 132 vehicles, cars or heavy weapons placements, he said. Al Jazeera could not independently verify the claims.

Yemeni government forces previously reclaimed Taiz’s Dhubab district and key positions near the critical Bab al-Mandeb strait.

Meanwhile, on the al-Jawf front, military engineering units continue to clear recaptured sites of mines and booby traps, al-Nazili added.

Late last month, the government said 16,100 Houthi operatives and commanders had been killed or wounded since October 5.

The Houthis have not confirmed a death toll and have in the meantime been firing missiles regularly towards Saudi Arabia, hitting multiple airports and disrupting air traffic over the kingdom.

Yazeed al-Jeddawy, a research manager at the Sana’a Center for Strategic Studies, told Al Jazeera that the course of the conflict increasingly appears to be moving towards a prolonged war of attrition as the government offensive has not shifted the balance of power over the past 30 days.

“The conflict is no longer driven solely by the dynamics inside Yemen; it is intertwined with the wider regional confrontation and the war involving Iran,” he added.

Prima ancora che cominci la battaglia degli emendamenti, c'è chi prepara quella degli striscioni contro la manovra. E poco importa se il governo ha convocato i sindacati a Palazzo Chigi per il 13 novembre. La protesta, infatti, continua a scandire il calendario delle tensioni: l'11 novembre scenderanno in piazza i sindacati della scuola, il 20 toccherà alla Cgil. E anche i poliziotti minacciano di scendere in strada per una previdenza dedicata che ancora non c'è.

Un malcontento che dai cancelli degli istituti e dalle questure raggiunge le stanze della maggioranza, dove sulle pensioni non c'è segno di conciliazione. La Lega non molla sull'uscita a 64 anni, trovando però in Lombardia il muro dell'assessore al Welfare Guido Bertolaso, che suggerisce di dirottare quelle risorse sugli ospedali. "Credo che oggi a 64 anni non ci voglia più andare nessuno in pensione, io ne sono un esempio", osserva, liquidando la bandiera del Carroccio.

Secca la replica dei leghisti lombardi: "Prima di fare politica sulle pensioni, Bertolaso faccia funzionare ciò che ha in carico". Un terreno previdenziale sul quale Forza Italia promette di muoversi anche per dare risposta agli uomini in divisa, con un intervento stimato in 48 milioni annui. La richiesta avrebbe trovato ascolto anche tra le fila di Fratelli d'Italia, con la Ragioneria incaricata di studiare una soluzione.

La prima miccia si accende tra i banchi di scuola: Cisl, Uil, Snals e Anief chiamano i lavoratori in piazza l'11 novembre, il 16 sarà la volta delle assemblee negli istituti, il 20 dello sciopero della Flc Cgil con università e ricerca. Nel mirino oltre 14mila posti tra docenti e Ata persi in tre anni, secondo la Cgil. Non si può rispondere al calo delle nascite svuotando le scuole, avvertono i sindacati. Lega e FI aprono, almeno a parole, a un "cambio di rotta". Più fredda FdI. .

E anche i costruttori dell'Ance presentano il conto al governo: mancano i fondi contro il caro materiali e gli ultimi crediti Superbonus vengono spalmati su dieci anni. Ma è sulla sanità che il conto si fa complesso: le Regioni avevano chiesto 6,5 miliardi aggiuntivi per il 2027, la manovra ne mette 2,4, oltre al miliardo già previsto. "La coperta, ahimè, è corta", ammette anche il governatore del Lazio e uomo del centrodestra, Francesco Rocca, reclamando risorse e flessibilità ma rinviando "i giudizi definitivi" alla fine dell'iter.

Una cautela che circola anche tra i giorgettiani della Lega, impegnati a gettare acqua sul fuoco e a fare scudo al ministro dell'Economia, da giorni bersaglio di rivendicazioni incrociate. A far rumore sono anche le divise, accusando il governo di aver "tradito la parola data" sulla previdenza dedicata. "Non è una pretesa di privilegio", spiega il segretario del Siulp, Felice Romano, evocando "una stagione di protesta senza precedenti". Fino all'avvertimento più delicato per un esecutivo che della sicurezza ha fatto una bandiera: "Stavolta nelle piazze manifesteranno i poliziotti".

A presidiare il dossier è FI - sotto l'egida del sottosegretario alla Difesa, Matteo Perego, e del senatore Maurizio Gasparri - che il 12 novembre incontrerà i sindacati per disinnescare la protesta, puntando anche sulla sponda Nato: le pensioni militari concorrono infatti al bilancio integrato della Difesa. E l'attivismo azzurro si allarga anche al fisco, con la richiesta di correggere l'exit tax sui super ricchi che lasciano il Paese, limitandola alle plusvalenze maturate in Italia e tutelando chi si trasferisce nell'Ue.

A offrire nuove munizioni alle opposizioni è invece il capitolo della difesa. Secondo Milex, nel 2027 la spesa militare supererà per la prima volta i 40 miliardi, destinando la cifra record di 17,2 miliardi agli armamenti. In due anni le risorse per le infrastrutture Nato e le forze di pronto intervento ammonteranno ad altri 865 milioni. Una manovra "da cestinare", la bolla Angelo Bonelli, puntando il dito contro la priorità data alle "armi" e non "al diritto alla salute". Una linea condivisa da Elly Schlein e rincarata da Giuseppe Conte: per le guerre si trovano miliardi, sostiene, ma non per i "progetti di vita".
