articles.body:
Max Justicz, the chief technology officer and co-founder of the startup Charge Robotics, used an OpenAI model to find a severe vulnerability that — if exploited — could allow hackers to take control of servers running Ubuntu, a widely used open source Linux-based operating system.

Justicz, who has a hobbyist’s interest in cybersecurity and previously found a vulnerability in the same codebase, told TechCrunch that he found this issue using GPT 5.6 Sol, released in July, through the AI maker’s Daybreak Blue, a program that gives cybersecurity defenders access to powerful frontier models.

“I literally just aimed ChatGPT at the same body of code and said ‘I found this bug previously that was fixed several years ago, please find bugs as bad or worse,’ and it came back in two hours with this,” Justicz said. “It’s extremely convoluted and hard for a human to find, but it works!”

He reported the issue to the Debian Project, which maintains the software in question and issued a patch to fix the vulnerability. There has been no known evidence of exploitation. Still, the ease with which he found it suggests that we’ve only seen the tip of the iceberg when it comes to potential exploits that even novice hackers can utilize with the help of AI models.

“I can only imagine what one could do with more time and access to less neutered models. We should expect some extremely crazy bugs to be found and exploited over the next few months,” Justicz wrote in a social media thread discussing his finding. “This might be obvious to most folks here, but there is currently huge alpha in taking some code or binary someone has not audited yet and just aiming a powerful AI model at it.”

OpenAI appears to have noticed. Today, the AI giant announced a new model focused on cybersecurity, ChatGPT Cyber, would be made available to the highest tier of users in the cybersecurity program, Daybreak Red, which allows offensive cybersecurity researchers tools for vulnerability hunting and development. Yesterday, OpenAI said that the same model had been used to scan and prepare patches for vulnerabilities in the Linux kernel, finding 948 potential issues. OpenAI also found 81 “novel” vulnerabilities in Firefox, the web browser.

“Our goal is to dramatically expand Daybreak, bringing advanced security research to organizations of every size, independent researchers, and open-source maintainers,” the frontier lab said in a statement.

OpenAI has insisted that there is a narrow window of time for the people who safeguard digital infrastructure to take action before AI models become even better at hacking and easier to access. For cyber defenders, however, it can feel like the frontier labs have unleashed a mountain of new work that outstrips their resources. Justicz said that he personally spent about $5,000 on subscriptions and tokens to find several exploits.

Besides Daybreak’s model access, OpenAI has also announced a $1 billion initiative to support cybersecurity professionals in the program who work on critical infrastructure like the electrical grid or water systems.

The Daybreak program has its own critiques. Justicz notes that the frontier lab appears to have recently “nerfed” Daybreak Blue to make it less useful at finding vulnerabilities. On one hand, it may be good to limit access from potential bad actors — Justicz said he just uploaded a photo of his driver’s license to join the program. On the other, cybersecurity professionals say they have one hand tied if they can’t use frontier technology while bad actors can deploy open-weight models with abliterated guardrails.

Still, OpenAI says just “thousands” of cybersecurity professionals are participating in the Daybreak program, versus a far larger number of potential hackers.

It’s unclear if frontier labs are devoting enough of their resources to this issue. Eric Wallace, a researcher on OpenAI’s technical staff, said that “we are now allocating a significant amount of our frontier compute towards discovering and patching vulnerabilities in open source codebases, fully pro bono.”

But the Linux bug hunt cost $1.2 million, which is significantly less than the approximate $6 million token spend the company invested in finding a potential solution to a famous problem of fluid dynamics.

If there is a narrow window of time to patch the digital infrastructure the world depends on, more urgency may be required.

articles.title: OpenAI president Greg Brockman says company could be IPO ready in 2027
articles.summary: Speaking at a Wall Street Journal tech conference on Wednesday, the executive touted how the company had been gaining ground in the enterprise market, where rival Anthropic had already successfully made inroads.
articles.preview: OpenAI co-founder and president Greg Brockman said the company would be ready for an IPO in 2027, noting that its enterprise revenue has been growing. Speaking at a Wall Street Journal tech conference on Wednesday, the executive touted how the company had been gaining ground in the enterprise market, where rival Anthropic had already successfully made inroads. In response to the interviewer’s question about being IPO-ready next year, Brockman replied, “I think so.
articles.body:
OpenAI co-founder and president Greg Brockman said the company would be ready for an IPO in 2027, noting that its enterprise revenue has been growing. Speaking at a Wall Street Journal tech conference on Wednesday, the executive touted how the company had been gaining ground in the enterprise market, where rival Anthropic had already successfully made inroads.

In response to the interviewer’s question about being IPO-ready next year, Brockman replied, “I think so. Yes.”

“We’ve been very clear this year that we want to go public when we feel is the right time for us, and I feel extremely good about the business. I feel like we’ve made so much progress this year, and I’ve honestly never felt more confident in what we’re doing,” Brockman said.

He detailed how OpenAI’s trajectory as an enterprise had changed over the course of 2026, noting that the first and second quarters were “pretty rough.” He also admitted that OpenAI “wasn’t even in the conversation” when it came to agentic coding — an area where Anthropic’s Claude Code has gained market share.

“We had Codex, but no one was talking about it,” Brockman continued, “and I think that we just kept our heads down and executed.”

By the third quarter, activity picked up, as OpenAI saw 70% quarterly growth in its annualized revenue — something Brockman attributed to the enterprise side of the business doubling. He explained that the growth wasn’t simply the result of something that happened in the quarter itself, but rather the culmination of investments the company had been making up to that point.

Now the majority of OpenAI’s revenue is coming from the enterprise business, which previously accounted for only around 30% of its total revenue.

“And it’s not that consumer [revenue has shrunk] … It’s been growing, but it’s the enterprise segment has really taken off,” he said, pointing to a recent partnership with JPMorgan Chase as one example of the type of client it’s now winning deals with.

Brockman also spoke more broadly about the lessons OpenAI learned from selling into the enterprise market as well. He said the company had come to understand that its job was to help businesses identify the most important milestones they could achieve with its AI technology, build trust with clients, and demonstrate that it was a reliable partner for the long haul.

“A year ago, we weren’t even really in the enterprise game, right? We were really perceived as a consumer company, and a lot of the companies we’d start talking to would say, ‘Is OpenAI really committed to the enterprise?’” Brockman said. “But it’s so different today.”

articles.title: L'Agenzia per la cybersicurezza: "Gli attacchi hacker ai frigo favoriti da software non aggiornati"
articles.summary: Il manager di un'azienda: 'La sicurezza informatica essenziale per catena del freddo'
articles.preview: Gli attacchi di questi giorni alle strutture refrigeranti della grande distribuzione sono stati facilitati dal fatto che questi frigo hanno "software non aggiornati o non più aggiornabili perché fuori mercato, e che presentano così delle vulnerabilità intrinseche", oltre alla "pratica della remotizzazione" di questi frigo. Lo afferma il direttore generale dell'Acn Andrea Quacivi in audizione alla commissione d'inchiesta sulle banche a seguito di una domanda del presidente Zanettin.
articles.body:
Gli attacchi di questi giorni alle strutture refrigeranti della grande distribuzione sono stati facilitati dal fatto che questi frigo hanno "software non aggiornati o non più aggiornabili perché fuori mercato, e che presentano così delle vulnerabilità intrinseche", oltre alla "pratica della remotizzazione" di questi frigo. Lo afferma il direttore generale dell'Acn Andrea Quacivi in audizione alla commissione d'inchiesta sulle banche a seguito di una domanda del presidente Zanettin.

Gli attacchi cyber alle banche una minaccia per la stabilità del sistema paese

"La minaccia cibernetica" al comparto bancario e assicurativo "è sempre più articolata e complessa e può produrre effetti sull'affidalità dei servizi, la fiducia dei cittadini e più in generale sulla stabilità del sistema paese". Lo afferma il dg dell'Acn Andrea Quacivi in audizione alla commissione d'inchiesta sulle banche servizi secondo cui queste minacce "sono sempre più articolate e complesse" con "modalità di attacco in continua evoluzione". Quacivi ha rilevato come il problema "non riguarda i singoli operatori ed è per questo essenziale "la collaborazione" fra istituzioni e autorità come l'Acn e la Banca d'Italia e altri.

La posta elettronica primo canale per attacchi a banche e assicurazioni

La posta elettronica è stato il canale privilegiato degli attacchi cyber a banche e assicurazioni "negli ultimi nove mesi". E' quanto ha affermato il dg dell'Acn Andrea Quacivi in audizione alla commissione d'inchiesta sul settore bancario e assicurativo secondo cui i criminali hanno poi utilizzato "credenziali rubate in precedenza e lo sfruttamento di vulnerabilità".

Quacivi ha sottolineato l'importanza strategica della sicurezza del settore banche e assicurazioni per il paese anche alla luce del crescente uso dell'Ia e della digitalizzazione del comparto. Il dg ha quindi ricordato come negli ultimi nove mesi si siano registrati per il settore "168 eventi cyber di cui 137 per le banche e 31 per assicurazioni, 15 al mese, fra questi 47 classificati come veri e propri incidenti eventi con impatto confermato". Inoltre per le banche "due terzi sono riconducibili alla criminalità e un terzo a gruppi attivisti" e altro.

Il Cremlino: 'Infondate le accuse sul coinvolgimento in attacchi ai supermercati'

Il portavoce presidenziale russo Dmitry Peskov ha definito "assurde" le accuse secondo cui gruppi di hacker filorussi sarebbero dietro i recenti attacchi informatici contro i sistemi di refrigerazione dei supermercati in alcuni Paesi europei. "Queste sono affermazioni assurde. Come sempre, non hanno fondamento, non hanno prove", ha dichiarato Peskov citato da Tass. "E queste accuse infondate contro il nostro Paese, di un coinvolgimento in tutto questo, purtroppo, stanno diventando una tendenza persistente nei Paesi europei", ha sottolineato il portavoce del Cremlino.

Gli esperti: 'Gli hacker russi avrebbero spiato gli smartphone tramite siti civetta'

Una campagna di spionaggio digitale attribuita "con un grado di certezza da moderato ad elevato" ai servizi segreti di Mosca avrebbe preso di mira gli iPhone e gli smartphone Android. A dirlo sono gli specialisti di sicurezza informatica dell'azienda Sekoia, che hanno svelato quella che sembra essere una rete di portali web manomessi o creati appositamente per ingannare gli utenti e installare programmi spia all'insaputa delle vittime. La trappola scatta nel momento in cui una persona visita uno dei siti controllati dal gruppo, noto agli analisti con la sigla Apt29.

Tra le esche figura una copia fittizia del portale ufficiale dedicato al 250/o anniversario dell'indipendenza degli Stati Uniti e la pagina del Raffles London at The Owo, un albergo di lusso situato nel cuore di Londra a breve distanza da Downing Street, già scelto come base per soggiorni diplomatici e visite di stato, compresa quella del presidente ucraino Zelensky. Per gli esperti, l'infezione è passata anche attraverso piattaforme compromesse legate all'Ucraina, tra cui una compagnia per l'estrazione di gas. Una volta sul portale civetta, un codice invisibile presente nella pagina web legge il modello e il sistema operativo in uso, per poi recapitare pacchetti malevoli capaci di colpire senza richiedere alcuna azione o conferma da parte dell'utente.

Tra questi strumenti figura anche DarkSword, commercializzato da società private di sorveglianza per sottrarre chiavi d'accesso delle reti wi-fi, dati di navigazione web e, nelle violazioni più profonde, l'intero archivio di file memorizzati sul dispositivo. Sekoia afferma che l'operazione non ha sfruttato nuove vulnerabilità ma difetti software già individuati e corretti da Apple e Google, ricordando l'importanza degli aggiornamenti come prima difesa contro le minacce informatiche.

M5S: 'Il governo spieghi come protegge i cittadini'

"Ho presentato un'interrogazione parlamentare rivolta alla presidente del Consiglio Meloni e al ministro Schillaci per sapere come il governo intenda agire a seguito degli attacchi hacker che hanno mandato in tilt gli impianti di refrigerazione di diversi supermercati in Italia, oltre che in altri paesi europei. Le recenti notizie emerse a seguito dei vertici che si sono tenuti in sede di governo non sembrano dare tutte le risposte necessarie. In particolare, mi sembrano evidenti i rischi anche in ambito sanitario e quindi per la salute dei cittadini italiani: in Francia, un attacco a un fornitore ha alterato i parametri delle celle frigorifere di tre sedi dell'Établissement français du sang nelle quali era conservato plasma". Lo afferma in una nota il deputato Alfonso Colucci, capogruppo in commissione Affari Costituzionali.

Con l'interrogazione chiediamo al governo se abbia promosso o intenda promuovere, d'intesa con le Regioni, verifiche presso i servizi trasfusionali e le farmacie ospedaliere per accertare che il personale possa rilevare tempestivamente, attraverso un sistema indipendente, un'alterazione della temperatura anche quando l'allarme centrale sia compromesso, e che siano disponibili procedure per trasferire in sicurezza emocomponenti e medicinali termolabili".

"Altri dubbi - aggiunge Colucci - rimangono anche sulla tutela degli alimenti nei negozi. Il 13 ottobre l'Agenzia per la cybersicurezza nazionale a seguito degli attacchi informatici agli impianti di refrigerazione di supermercati francesi, aveva raccomandato agli operatori italiani di verificare con urgenza la sicurezza degli accessi da remoto. Purtroppo però gli attacchi hacker sono arrivati anche in alcuni punti vendita italiani e il 3 novembre l'Agenzia ha riproposto il bollettino. Chiediamo di sapere dal governo quali verifiche siano state svolte dopo il bollettino del 13 ottobre, con quali esiti e quali iniziative siano state adottate per raggiungere anche le piccole imprese e i fornitori che gestiscono da remoto gli impianti di più strutture. Vogliamo inoltre sapere quante segnalazioni siano pervenute ai NAS, quali controlli siano stati eseguiti sulla conservazione degli alimenti e se, nei casi in cui non fosse possibile documentare il rispetto delle temperature prescritte, sia stata verificata la destinazione dei prodotti interessati".

articles.title: India flags Chinese-linked AI tools in hacking campaign against financial firms
articles.summary: India's cybersecurity agency said the attackers used publicly available AI tools to automate break-ins "at machine speed", calling the threat "active and ongoing".
articles.preview: India's cybersecurity agency said the attackers used publicly available AI tools to automate break-ins "at machine speed", calling the threat "active and ongoing". BENGALURU/MUMBAI: India's cybersecurity agency named the hacking group behind a wave of AI-driven attacks on financial firms and identified its tools, at least two of them linked to China, adding India to a growing list of countries where such tools have been used against banks.
articles.body:
India's cybersecurity agency said the attackers used publicly available AI tools to automate break-ins "at machine speed", calling the threat "active and ongoing".

BENGALURU/MUMBAI: India's cybersecurity agency named the hacking group behind a wave of AI-driven attacks on financial firms and identified its tools, at least two of them linked to China, adding India to a growing list of countries where such tools have been used against banks.

The group, which the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) calls "Crafty Falcon," has breached non-bank lenders, fintech firms and cryptocurrency exchanges, according to an advisory issued on Wednesday (Nov 4).

CERT-In did not say who was behind the breaches or where the organisation operates.

The advisory came after a spate of cyberattacks on Indian banks and non-bank lenders in recent weeks, even as authorities issued warnings and the Reserve Bank of India tightened cybersecurity checks.

CERT-In said the attackers use publicly available AI tools to automate break-ins "at machine speed", calling the threat "active and ongoing".

It named four tools: ARTEX, PentAGI, Cairn and CyberStrikeAI. Security researchers have linked at least two of them to China.

China-made ARTEX has been used in attacks on South Korean banks since late September, cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike has said.

It said a China-linked group also used the tool in an espionage campaign targeting more than 200 organisations in at least 14 countries.

CERT-In did not name the affected companies or say how much money was stolen.

The agency did not say the attacks were state-sponsored and the tools it named have been freely available online. ARTEX, however, was made private by its developer last month after it was linked to the South Korean attacks.

CERT-In, the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre and India's IT ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

PAYMENT INTERFACES TARGETED

CERT-In said Crafty Falcon "surveys its targets with machine intelligence" and moves money by invoking victims' own payment and disbursement systems.

Attacks were timed around holidays, weekends and other low-monitoring periods to delay detection. Firms that had fixed flaws after earlier alerts were attacked again after incomplete remediations were made, it said.

Reuters previously reported, citing a police complaint, that last month two Mumbai-based non-bank lenders lost about US$2 million in more than 700 unauthorised instant transfers from accounts of India's third-largest lender ICICI Bank on Oct 8 and 9.

The complaint said hackers compromised its application programming interfaces (APIs), the software links banks use to connect with non-bank lenders and fintech firms to send loan-disbursal instructions.

State Bank of India, the country's largest lender, disclosed a dark-web leak of 3,897 customer records last month. Spandana Sphoorty Financial, a non-bank lender, reported unauthorised debits from a bank account on Nov 1, and AU Small Finance Bank said it was probing a potential customer-data leak.

CERT-In did not say which incidents were linked to Crafty Falcon.

articles.title: China blocks SoftBank’s $5.4 billion ABB robot unit takeover
articles.summary: The takeover was widely expected to bolster SoftBank's revenue and profit while it awaits a boost from OpenAI's public debut.
articles.preview: China has blocked the sale of ABB’s robotics unit to SoftBank Group, dealing a blow to the Japanese investment firm’s plans to expand into physical AI. A Chinese government agency blocked the $5.4 billion deal, ABB said in an emailed statement. The takeover was widely expected to bolster SoftBank’s revenue and profit while it awaits a boost from OpenAI’s public debut. SoftBank’s shares were down around 7% in Tokyo on Thursday. A company spokesperson declined to comment.
articles.body:
China has blocked the sale of ABB’s robotics unit to SoftBank Group, dealing a blow to the Japanese investment firm’s plans to expand into physical AI.

A Chinese government agency blocked the $5.4 billion deal, ABB said in an emailed statement. The takeover was widely expected to bolster SoftBank’s revenue and profit while it awaits a boost from OpenAI’s public debut.

SoftBank’s shares were down around 7% in Tokyo on Thursday. A company spokesperson declined to comment.

Founder Masayoshi Son has listed the deal as a key part of his ambition to play a larger role in the artificial intelligence buildout. The Tokyo-based firm was looking to take over a business from Swiss-Swedish conglomerate ABB with more than 7,000 employees, which supplies robotic arms and industrial machinery to manufacturers like BMW and has a large presence in China.

Investors worry about Son’s commitments to AI, from SoftBank’s near-$65 billion bet on OpenAI to pledges of hundreds of billions of dollars on data center projects. Some had looked to ABB’s expected contribution to SoftBank’s bottom line for assurance that the company was not overextending itself.

“ABB Robotics lacks the cutting-edge innovation found across SoftBank’s physical AI startup portfolio, but its domain expertise and manufacturing knowhow had been expected to transform robotic concepts into actual businesses,” said Bloomberg Intelligence analyst Kirk Boodry.

Beijing’s move against the ABB deal casts more uncertainty over SoftBank’s ambitions, and reflects the Chinese government’s renewed emphasis on safeguarding its data and technology in the AI era.

In April, China’s powerful National Development and Reform Commission blocked Meta Platforms’s $2 billion acquisition of agentic AI startup Manus, issuing a one-line notice saying it had decided to prohibit foreign investment in the startup in accordance with laws and regulations.

SoftBank’s acquisition was similarly subjected to a foreign investment security review by the state planner, according to an earlier report in the Financial Times. China’s Office of the Working Mechanism for Foreign Investment Security Review prohibited the deal, according to the ABB statement.

Beijing, recognizing how data is the foundation of artificial intelligence, has this year clamped down on the transfer of vital information abroad. That’s true also of the robotics arena, where data is fundamental to eventually making robots work.

Japan is home to many of the world’s biggest industrial robot makers including Fanuc, Yaskawa Electric and Kawasaki Heavy Industries. Most have partnered with Nvidia to explore ways to use AI inside factories, hospitals and logistics networks and stay ahead of rising competition from China.

articles.title: Da Binance agli smartphone, gli hacker mettono nel mirino i 'wallet digitali'
articles.summary: Asaro (Polimi): 'I pagamenti con smartphone sicuri, ma servono buone abitudini'
articles.preview: Dai caveau digitali della finanza decentralizzata fino ai chip contactless custoditi nei telefoni personali, il baricentro del crimine informatico ha cambiato traiettoria. Il bersaglio principale non è più il singolo codice di pagamento o una credenziale isolata ma l'accesso e la gestione dei portafogli digitali, i cosiddetti "wallet". A confermarlo è la cronaca recente, segnata dall'attacco sferrato contro l'infrastruttura di Binance. Ma anche i consumatori fuori dal circuito delle criptovalute rischiano, come dimostra una recente ricerca di NordVpn.
articles.body:
Dai caveau digitali della finanza decentralizzata fino ai chip contactless custoditi nei telefoni personali, il baricentro del crimine informatico ha cambiato traiettoria. Il bersaglio principale non è più il singolo codice di pagamento o una credenziale isolata ma l'accesso e la gestione dei portafogli digitali, i cosiddetti "wallet".

A confermarlo è la cronaca recente, segnata dall'attacco sferrato contro l'infrastruttura di Binance. Ma anche i consumatori fuori dal circuito delle criptovalute rischiano, come dimostra una recente ricerca di NordVpn. Per gli esperti, sul dark web nell'ultimo anno le conversazioni dedicate al furto di carte di pagamento da caricare direttamente sui wallet dei criminali sono quasi triplicate.

Le carte già predisposte per l'utilizzo su piattaforme Apple e Google vengono vendute sulla parte oscura della rete a un prezzo tra il 3% e il 5% del saldo disponibile sul conto associato, a cui aggiungere il costo delle informazioni personali, senza le quali non è possibile utilizzare il sistema in maniera fraudolenta. "Pagare con lo smartphone e con portafogli digitali online è sempre più semplice e sicuro", spiega all'ANSA Ivano Asaro, Direttore dell'Osservatorio Innovative Payments del Politecnico di Milano, "ma è importante conoscere e praticare alcune buone abitudini".

Per NordVpn, una tessera corredata del numero di previdenza sociale o codice fiscale e della data di nascita del titolare ha un prezzo medio di 18,15 dollari, con picchi di 23 dollari. Una carta senza riferimenti sensibili si attesta invece sugli 11 dollari. I truffatori intercettano i codici monouso (otp) ricorrendo al "vishing", la telefonata in cui un finto operatore bancario convince l'utente a fornire le cifre appena ricevute, l'uso improprio di nome e cognome per superare i controlli della banca e il "sim swapping", ovvero il trasferimento del numero di cellulare sulla scheda del truffatore così da intercettare gli sms di verifica.

"Non bisogna mai comunicare al telefono codici di sicurezza, pin o credenziali, anche se chi chiama dice di essere della banca o un nostro amico, considerando che la sua voce potrebbe essere replicata con l'intelligenza artificiale", dice Asaro, "la fiducia nei pagamenti digitali si costruisce anche così: con tecnologie sicure e consumatori informati".

articles.title: Mattarella: "Urgente una difesa comune europea"
articles.summary: AGI - Procedere con urgenza in direzione di una difesa comune europea. L’appello, reiterato, da parte del Presidente della Repubblica arriva nel giorno in cui si celebrano l’ Unità nazionale e le Forze Armate . Ricorrenza che acquista quest’anno un carico emotivo particolare, per la scomparsa dei quattro militari italiani in Bosnia , ma anche alla luce delle recenti minacce cyber che hanno colpito la cosiddetta “catena del freddo”, in Europa e in Italia. Il messaggio al ministro della Difesa Non sembra un caso, infatti, che il Capo dello Stato sottolinei nel messaggio inviato al ministro della Difesa il fatto che ai “conflitti tradizionali, che continuano a insanguinare ampie aree del mondo, inclusa l’Europa si aggiungono la disinformazione diffusa, la competizione nello spazio, la dimensione cibernetica, l’uso pervasivo dell’intelligenza artificiale e dei sistemi autonomi, domini in cui atti di aggressione risultano oggi in preoccupante e progressiva espansione”. Lo sforzo europeo Concetto ribadito a poche ore dall’incontro di ieri al Quirinale con gli allievi degli Istituti di formazione militare, in occasione della cerimonia di conferimento delle decorazioni all’Ordine militare d’Italia. “In questo contesto è necessario uno sforzo europeo più concreto e più integrato, determinato nel perseguire una interoperabilità degli strumenti militari dei Paesi dell’Unione, in chiave di difesa comune e di rafforzamento dell’Alleanza Atlantica, condizioni imprescindibili per l’equilibrio delle condizioni nel continente”, aveva sottolineato Mattarella. Uno scenario, riprende oggi il Capo dello Stato, “che richiede profonda capacità di rinnovamento, nell’integrare rapidamente le nuove tecnologie e nel garantire capacità concrete per le sfide future”. La Costituzione e la memoria Il tutto nella cornice imprescindibile della Carta Costituzionale, di cui il Presidente della Repubblica è il primo custode: “Il giuramento di fedeltà delle Forze Armate alla Repubblica si nutre dei valori della sua Costituzione”, dice Mattarella, “patrimonio di principi custodito affinché il rapporto con le generazioni che si succedono nella vita del Paese sappia unire la memoria del passato alla speranza per il futuro della comunità, e le atrocità vissute nelle guerre mondiali non abbiano a ripetersi”. Le cerimonie e il cordoglio per i militari in Bosnia Il messaggio di Mattarella precede la cerimonia all’Altare della Patria, prima, e quella a Piazzale Michelangelo, a Firenze, poi. Qui il Presidente della Repubblica ha ritrovato il Generale di Corpo d’Armata e Capo di Stato maggiore della Difesa, Luciano Portolano al quale ha ribadito anche oggi il “profondo cordoglio” e la “grande commozione” per la morte dei quattro militari Italiani nell’incidente in elicottero in Bosnia. “In questa giornata, il deferente omaggio del popolo italiano va a quanti hanno sacrificato la vita per l’Italia, consegnandoci un’eredità di libertà e unità che celebriamo con rinnovata consapevolezza e, oggi, rivolgiamo il nostro pensiero con particolare intensità e cordoglio ai nostri militari che hanno perso la vita nei giorni scorsi in Bosnia-Erzegovina”, le parole di Mattarella. “Celebriamo questa giornata con orgoglio di sempre ma oggi col dolore e col cuore pesante per il lutto che ci ha colpito in Bosnia”, ha esordito Portolano prima di soffermarsi, così come il Capo dello Stato, sulle nuove minacce che impegnano le Forze Armate. Se un secolo fa, ha ricordato il generale di Corpo d’Armata, le linee da difendere avevano un nome, quella del Grappa o quella del Piave, oggi ci troviamo di fronte a nuove e numerose linee da difendere, ha sottolineato. articles.title: Commentary: Who keeps crashing China’s stock market?
articles.summary: Over the past decade, the domestic market has endured at least three bear runs that prompted emergency government bailouts, says Shuli Ren for Bloomberg Opinion.
articles.preview: Over the past decade, the domestic market has endured at least three bear runs that prompted emergency government bailouts, says Shuli Ren for Bloomberg Opinion. HONG KONG: China is scrambling to contain a stock market rout only two years after the previous rescue. Beijing is dusting off the market support playbook it deployed in 2024. The People’s Bank of China (PBOC) is providing low-cost funding for corporate share buybacks and liquidity for institutional investors.
articles.body:
Over the past decade, the domestic market has endured at least three bear runs that prompted emergency government bailouts, says Shuli Ren for Bloomberg Opinion.

HONG KONG: China is scrambling to contain a stock market rout only two years after the previous rescue.

Beijing is dusting off the market support playbook it deployed in 2024. The People’s Bank of China (PBOC) is providing low-cost funding for corporate share buybacks and liquidity for institutional investors. The shadowy “national team” appears to have stepped up its operations, while regulators are again resorting to window guidance – informally instructing institutional investors and brokerages not to sell.

In October, China’s stock market suffered its worst monthly decline in more than a decade. The blue-chip CSI 300 Index has fallen into a bear market from its late-June peak, while Shanghai’s semiconductor-heavy SSE Science and Technology Innovation Board 50 Index, or Star 50, has plunged as much as 48 per cent.

THE BLAME GAME

So who’s been selling? The blame game has already begun.

Shiva Capital Group, one of China’s biggest hedge funds, has pointed the finger at insurers. In a recent letter to clients, founder Hong Liang accused the insurance firms of piling into technology stocks near their July peak, only to slash positions in late September. The behaviour was “truly baffling”, lamented the prominent investor, who has a large following on the mainland.

Liang certainly has reason to deflect blame. China has a long history of faulting private sector investors, from quant funds to foreign asset managers, for igniting selloffs. But he might just have a point this time.

China had already endured a bear market in July, when momentum-driven trades suffered their worst loss in history. The pattern mirrored markets in South Korea and the United States, where the red-hot semiconductor trade was hastily unwound.

NOT THE USUAL SUSPECTS

Three months later, however, the usual suspects are harder to blame. Margin financing has already fallen, as has northbound turnover through the Stock Connect with Hong Kong, suggesting neither leveraged traders nor foreign hot money is behind the latest weakness.

That leaves a different potential offender: long-only institutional investors.

State-owned insurers have been steadily increasing their stock holdings in recent years. China Life Insurance, for instance, has scaled up artificial-intelligence-related bets and raised its equity allocation to 19.2 per cent of its portfolio by the end of June, from 16.9 per cent in 2025.

Beyond the hunt for higher returns, insurers have been responding to policymakers, who want them to provide more long-term capital to the stock market – a priority that the head of China’s securities regulator reiterated in a high-profile speech in mid-June. Talk about bad timing.

In recent days, authorities have issued window guidance to several major insurers, requiring them to report their equity holdings, refrain from cutting their losses, and align investment decisions with broader economic goals.

WHO WILL BE LEFT TO BLAME?

The government now appears to be grappling with an unintended consequence of its own policy.

Insurers may be more patient investors than hedge funds, but they still have to manage risk and meet claims and other liabilities. That limits their ability to sit indefinitely on mounting losses – and can force them to cut exposure during severe market downturns.

Insurers, in other words, cannot be as reliably countercyclical as the “national team”, whose primary purpose is market stabilisation.

On its latest earnings call, executives at China Pacific Insurance Group acknowledged that equity investing had become “complicated” and that portfolios needed to be managed so market volatility didn’t damage short-term returns. In the third quarter, profits at China’s five major listed insurers plunged, largely because of the decline in domestic stocks.

The experience points to an uncomfortable reality: For insurers, reliable dividend payers such as Bank of Jiangsu may ultimately be better suited to their liabilities than capital-intensive chipmakers.

Few in China – including Shiva’s Liang – are willing to say publicly that policy missteps themselves may be contributing to poor stock market performance. Instead, blame has fallen on everything from thin liquidity to indiscriminate selling.

But that raises a bigger question: Why does China keep suffering stock market routs? Over the past decade, the domestic market has endured at least three bear runs that prompted emergency government bailouts – in 2018, 2024 and now.

The next time the PBOC has to put out a fire, who will be left to blame? Foreigners, hedge funds and now even state-owned insurers have all had their turn.

articles.title: Lagarde: 'A dicembre capiremo se dovremo alzare ancora i tassi'
articles.summary: L'inflazione italiana supera il 4% a causa dell'energia'
articles.preview: La presidente della Bce Christine Lagarde, in uscita anticipata per potersi "esprimere più liberamente" non esclude nulla in tema di tassi. A dicembre, in quello che sarà molto probabilmente l'ultimo consiglio che presiederà sull'argomento, la Banca Centrale Europea valuterà infatti se ritoccare il costo del denaro. Lo afferma davanti a una platea di oltre 600 studenti invitati in Piazza Affari dall'Osservatorio for Indipendent Thinking nell'ambito del progetto 'Young Factor' sull'educazione finanziaria.
articles.body:
La presidente della Bce Christine Lagarde, in uscita anticipata per potersi "esprimere più liberamente" non esclude nulla in tema di tassi. A dicembre, in quello che sarà molto probabilmente l'ultimo consiglio che presiederà sull'argomento, la Banca Centrale Europea valuterà infatti se ritoccare il costo del denaro. Lo afferma davanti a una platea di oltre 600 studenti invitati in Piazza Affari dall'Osservatorio for Indipendent Thinking nell'ambito del progetto 'Young Factor' sull'educazione finanziaria.

"Nell'ultima riunione di politica monetaria - spiega - abbiamo discusso se alzare nuovamente i tassi, ma abbiamo ritenuto di essere ben posizionati per aspettare e vedere quali numeri, dati e informazioni arriveranno". "Rivedremo le nostre proiezioni a dicembre - chiarisce - quando avremo molti indicatori che ci aiuteranno davvero a determinare se un rialzo sia necessario per conseguire il nostro obiettivo".

Lagarde ricorda che l'inflazione al 4% nell'area euro e superiore al 5% in Italia è alimentata prevalentemente dall'energia, con rincari su base annua rispettivamente del 18% e di oltre il 20%.

"Poiché l'energia entra in moltissime delle cose che facciamo - argomenta - ha spinto verso l'alto l'insieme dei prezzi. Questa situazione probabilmente proseguirà per un certo periodo, fino all'emergere di un effetto base nel confronto annuo. Dico probabilmente sottolineandolo molto - precisa - perché le cose cambiano estremamente in fretta".

Una dinamica, quella dei prezzi legata all'energia, che per l'Italia vale ancora di più: "è come il motore di un auto - spiega - devi aprire il cofano e vedere come mai il dato è così alto".

"Principalmente - sottolinea - è colpa dell'energia, il cui prezzo in Italia è aumentato del 20%". Ai giovani Lagarde invita ad elaborare un "pensiero critico e libero" e ricorda che alla base della propria decisione di lasciare in anticipo c'è proprio la volontà di potersi "esprimere liberamente".

"Nelle circostanze attuali - sottolinea - in Europa e altrove voglio poter esprimere con maggiore indipendenza opinioni in cui credo fermamente e partecipare a dibattiti che non riguardano la politica monetaria". "Avrei comunque terminato a ottobre - chiarisce - perché questa è la regola: come presidente della Bce hai un mandato di 8 anni e alla fine non c'è rinnovo, non si prolunga: si va via, e basta e quello che ho fatto è stato anticipare di 9 mesi quell'uscita inevitabile".

articles.body:
When will Australia see the benefits of the AI and datacentre boom? So far, all we’ve seen is the possibility of changes to copyright that would hurt Australian creatives, special rules about power and water use, and the threat of mass displacement or replacement of workers, with the trade-off being a mere 10% chance of human extinction.

Now add the Reserve Bank’s assessment this week that datacentres were part of growing “inflationary pressures” when lifting interest rates to an 18-year high.

Warnings about looming negatives have been coming for months, but even the RBA has no idea when to expect the positives. And, as the results of the US midterms show us, datacentres are becoming political kryptonite for voters not sold on the AI boom, meaning the Albanese government should tread carefully.

As Labor mulls its long-awaited plan to attract AI investment, this week’s RBA decision demands politicians better explain what the benefits of this rollout will be, and why it is worth the (hopefully short-term) pain. It also requires the government to consider other inflation responses, beyond the RBA.

The governor, Michele Bullock, warned “some pain now will prevent even worse pain” in the future. But why should ordinary workers endure pain that is not of their own making?

Some of the richest companies in the world are helping heat the economy to such an extent that Bullock flagged it in her opening remarks, just moments after pointing to global oil prices, low productivity and expectations of prolonged inflation.

“Parts of demand have also been stronger than expected. In particular, investment has been much stronger than expected, including due to datacentre-related investment,” she said. “This has added to inflationary pressures by adding to demand at a time when the domestic economy is already capacity constrained.”

The RBA’s statement of monetary policy highlighted that “AI-related investment is driving rapid growth in prices for technology-related goods” in its second paragraph.

But asked when AI would start having a “positive impact on inflation”, Bullock shrugged “your guess is as good as mine”.

She said “if productivity improves dramatically because of AI” – “if”, not “when” – then we would see faster growth, but also warned it could increase the “neutral interest rate”.

“So if people think that productivity improvements will help to lower inflation and keep interest rates low, that’s not necessarily the case,” Bullock said.

Even the nation’s chief economic wonk is hazy on when the benefits start flowing.

These aren’t nimby arguments against datacentres or luddite concerns about technological growth; there are serious economic questions to be considered here, and social ones already being examined worldwide.

Deloitte Access Economics on Thursday reported Australia’s $1.39tn investment pipeline included 37 datacentres worth $141bn – a 36% increase in a year.

Deloitte director Sheraan Underwood said the datacentre boom was “competing directly with housing and infrastructure for workers and materials” and that Australia had “less room to absorb” the investment surge thanks to high inflation.

Deloitte reported “the economic dividend may take time”, predicting “substantial” construction gains but that the “direct economic payoff” wouldn’t be as big. The technology fit-out is largely imported goods and few workers are needed to actually staff the facilities.

Of course the datacentre boom will support AI takeup, greater automation and productivity, but Deloitte warned: “Construction demand and inflation pressures are arriving now, while the productivity dividend may come much later.”

After RBA warnings about demand, much media focus has naturally turned to government spending. Press gallery pundits have zeroed in, particularly, on green subsidies and home batteries; the shadow energy minister, Dan Tehan, blasted a “blowout” from a budgeted $2.3bn to $8.5bn.

That’s $6.2bn more than budgeted. Or, in another way, 4% of the total $141bn datacentre investment.

Or 16% of the growth in datacentre investment in just one year.

Economics and finance, like politics, is a series of choices. If everything is on the table for savings, as Labor has said, shouldn’t we consider the benefits of untrammelled investment in AI factories before we start slashing social programs achieving good?

This week’s datacentre backlash in the United States is instructive. Politico recently reported polling showing half of Americans oppose datacentres near their homes; NBC exit polls found 56% of voters said AI and datacentres were “crucial” or “major” factors in the midterms. Datacentres were also literally on the ballot in dozens of towns, with public votes overwhelmingly won by proposals to restrict construction, according to vote trackers.

The Australian backlash is much smaller, but growing. Community groups are organising and protesting. Labor should not overlook bubbling voter unease.

So what to do instead? Beyond leaving it to the “blunt instrument” of monetary policy for the RBA to smash the economy, there are other options Labor could consider. They are novel, but the times demand novel solutions.

Senator David Pocock has proposed a Senate committee to investigate “alternatives” to monetary policy, suggesting options including “temporary, progressive” changes to income tax or superannuation. Independent economist Saul Eslake has said a small rise in superannuation rates, from even 12% to 13%, would take some money out of workers’ pockets and help curb spending. Pocock, again, suggested taxes on windfall profits and gas exports to take more cash out of the economy.

Of course we need new AI and datacentre investment, particularly as the government looks for a magic bullet to end stagnant productivity. But the government has so far struggled to make the case for how this new technology will benefit ordinary Australians, who are left with a feeling of uncertainty and a hole in their back pocket.

articles.title: What the Democrats' midterms win means for the US economy and Trump
articles.summary: From high oil prices and data centers to tariffs and mounting debt, economic concerns played a key role in the crushing defeat of President Donald Trump's Republicans. So can the Democrats now make a difference?
articles.preview: November 5, 2026 From high oil prices and data centers to tariffs and mounting debt, economic concerns played a key role in the crushing defeat of President Donald Trump's Republicans. So can the Democrats now make a difference? For the millions who cast their ballots in the US midterm elections, one issue ranked above all others: the economy. So what does the Democrats' stunning capture of both the US Senate and House of Representatives mean for the economy and economic policy, given that President Donald Trump still has two years of his term to go?
articles.body:
November 5, 2026

From high oil prices and data centers to tariffs and mounting debt, economic concerns played a key role in the crushing defeat of President Donald Trump's Republicans. So can the Democrats now make a difference?

For the millions who cast their ballots in the US midterm elections, one issue ranked above all others: the economy.

So what does the Democrats' stunning capture of both the US Senate and House of Representatives mean for the economy and economic policy, given that President Donald Trump still has two years of his term to go?

Market reaction: Is it all about AI and data centers?

Markets have rebounded after initially trending negatively. Global stocks rallied as investors appeared to take heart from the Democrats' victory.

With Democrats now holding comfortable majorities in both houses of Congress and Trump still in the White House, it could lead to gridlock in Washington. Trump has already said he would become "Mr Veto," meaning he would block any legislation the Democrats advance.

"The magnitude of the gains for the Democrats in the midterms does not change too much for the near-term policy outlook, given the party still lacks a filibuster-proof majority in the Senate and President Trump has veto power to block legislation," Stephen Brown, chief North America economist with Capital Economics, said in a note.

"I think we are looking at two years of complete 100% gridlock," Jacob Funk Kirkegaard, nonresident senior fellow with the Peterson Institute for International Economics, told DW after the results came in. "Nothing will get done of any kind."

Some investors appear worried that the Democrats could force through AI regulation, especially if they also win the White House in 2028. Rising opposition among large majorities of the US population to data centers — the key infrastructure behind AI — helped secure victories for many Democratic candidates.

Kirkegaard, who is also a senior fellow at Bruegel, a European economics think tank, said the vote showed the extent of that opposition. Even if the Democrats can't force regulation, he thinks local opposition will make it harder for data centers to be built, which could hit the valuation of big tech firms that have benefitted from the AI boom.

"This election shows that the political underpinning of the rapid, aggressive AI growth story is shaky," he said. "It doesn't mean it's going to stop or be made illegal, but the dynamic of the growth story has shifted."

If the Democrats were to win the presidency in 2028, Brown said, they would be perfectly placed to make major policy changes. "That includes the potential for tax hikes on corporations and high-income individuals as well as regulation that could delay the AI rollout," he said.

What about Trump's tariff policies?

According to polling conducted in early October by the Pew Research Center, 56% of Americans say Trump's tariff policies will have mostly negative impacts on the country, with only 20% saying mostly positive.

That sentiment clearly drove many Democrats to victory in the midterms — particularly in states where tariffs have had a particularly negative impact. That includes those with sectors reliant on exports, such as Texas, Michigan, Iowa and Illinois, where counter-tariffs have hit and those that have high trade volumes with Canada.

Yet, barring an unprecedented climbdown from Trump — who has been ideologically wedded to tariffs since he first became a public figure almost 50 years ago — it's not clear how the Democrats could force substantial change to the president's signature economic policy.

"Trump will not be moderated," Deborah Elms, head of trade policy at the Hinrich Foundation in Singapore, told DW earlier this year. "Expect him to continue his trade disruption and tariff policies for as long as he remains in the Oval Office."

Though the US Constitution gives Congress the power to collect and organize tariffs, various laws passed over the years have given presidents power to implement tariffs when they cite certain conditions, such as national security or economic emergencies.

Trump has already used such avenues for his tariffs and can continue to do so, despite some legal rebukes. However, while Congress can't necessarily force an end to Trump's existing tariffs, it can now take further legal action against them to prevent greater escalation.

What about the war in Iran and surging oil prices?

Though Trump and the Democrats are clearly not going to make common cause, Kirkegaard said, the scale of the Republicans' defeat might force Trump to be less erratic in his policymaking, from escalating his trade war with Canada to his Iran policy.

Trump said in the aftermath of Tuesday's defeats that he would "work with" the Democrats and told the Financial Times in the run-up to the vote that he was unlikely to escalate the war in Iran.

Were a deal to be struck with Iran, soaring energy prices — a pivotal election issue — could finally fall, helping voters with their cost-of-living concerns.

"You've got to get a deal with Iran, and you've got to bring down gas prices," Kirkegaard said. "From a political point of view, that's the most important thing now."

George Saravelos, an analyst with Deutsche Bank FX Research, thinks the markets are beginning to become more optimistic in that area. "With oil flows through the Middle East having materially recovered, the market is pricing a large imminent risk premium of re-escalation and energy supply disruption," he said in a note.

Could Democrats force Trump to table on the economy?

Despite the scale of the Democrats' victory, the fact that Trump remains in the Oval Office will complicate all efforts to force a change to signature economic policies and issues.

Yet Congress can now exert considerable pressure. Another issue vital to voters was corruption and the belief that the Trump administration has engaged in corruption and personal enrichment while in office.

That raises the prospect of the new Democratic-controlled Congress launching legal investigations and potentially pursuing another impeachment of Trump, which could force the president to negotiate on some economic issues to secure his political survival.

"Can you find 10 or 12 Republican senators who, in the face of overwhelming corruption, would be willing to vote for articles of impeachment? I wouldn't rule it out," Kirkegaard said. "And that's a scenario in which Trump might suddenly be much more accommodating to, for instance, abandoning most of his tariffs."

Despite voters' clear rejection of Trump's economic policies, the Democratic Party's newly minted senators, congressmen and congresswomen face an uphill battle in trying to reverse them.

articles.title: Rwe investe un miliardo in Italia, oltre metà nell’eolico

È il programma di Rwe, gruppo energetico tedesco e uno dei principali operatori delle rinnovabili nel Paese, del quale si è parlato nei giorni scorsi a Enna in occasione dell’inaugurazione dell’impianto agrivoltaico avanzato da 9,5 MWac.
articles.body:
Circa un miliardo di euro di investimenti in Italia tra il 2026 e il 2031, con più della metà delle risorse destinate all’eolico e la parte restante a fotovoltaico, agrivoltaico e batterie. È il programma di Rwe, gruppo energetico tedesco e uno dei principali operatori delle rinnovabili nel Paese, del quale si è parlato nei giorni scorsi a Enna in occasione dell’inaugurazione dell’impianto agrivoltaico avanzato da 9,5 MWac.

La società dispone in Italia di circa 670 MW installati, distribuiti tra 18 parchi eolici onshore, un impianto fotovoltaico e tre agrivoltaici in esercizio. Altri 200 MW sono in costruzione attraverso progetti eolici e fotovoltaici. L’obiettivo è raggiungere un gigawatt di capacità installata entro il 2030, ampliando la produzione nazionale e diversificando le tecnologie.

«Prevediamo di investire circa 1 miliardo di euro in Italia nel periodo 2026-2031, destinando più della metà dell’investimento all’eolico e la restante parte a progetti fotovoltaici, inclusi quelli agrivoltaici, e a sistemi di accumulo a batterie - dice Paolo Raia, Country Chair Rwe Renewables Italia -. Lo sviluppo integrato di queste tecnologie è fondamentale per sostenere la crescita delle rinnovabili e contribuire a un sistema elettrico nazionale più flessibile, resiliente e sicuro. Attraverso questi investimenti, vogliamo contribuire concretamente al percorso di decarbonizzazione e alla sicurezza energetica del Paese, generando al tempo stesso valore duraturo per i territori e le comunità in cui operiamo».

La struttura italiana conta oltre 200 dipendenti, tra responsabili di progetto, ingegneri, tecnici e operatori, con uffici a Milano e Roma. Le attività coprono l’intera vita degli impianti: dall’individuazione dei siti allo sviluppo, dalla costruzione alla manutenzione, fino alla dismissione o al repowering. L’eolico resta la componente principale del portafoglio, che comprende, tra gli altri, Morcone da 57 MW, San Severo da 54 MW e Mondonuovo da 53,1 MW. Tra le entrate in esercizio più recenti figura Serra Palino, in Puglia, da 47 MW.

L’altro passaggio è la crescita dell’agrivoltaico. In Italia Rwe ha realizzato i suoi primi impianti commerciali di agrivoltaico avanzato a livello mondiale. Il portafoglio comprende Morcone, da 9,8 MWac, e Acquafredda, da 9,3 MWac, ai quali si è aggiunto Enna. Altri due impianti agrivoltaici sono previsti in esercizio nelle prossime settimane. In Sicilia è operativo anche il fotovoltaico Bosco, indicato nella documentazione aziendale con una capacità di nove MWac.

articles.body:
Indonesia has contended with weaker investor sentiment this year amid heightened scrutiny of the government's fiscal plans and its broader policy directions.

JAKARTA: Indonesia's economy expanded 5.47 per cent in the third quarter from a year earlier, official data showed on Thursday (Nov 5), faster than the 5.18 per cent forecast in a Reuters poll.

Indonesia's economic growth in the second quarter stood at 5.29 per cent.

Southeast Asia's largest economy has contended with weaker investor sentiment this year amid heightened scrutiny of the government's fiscal plans and its broader policy directions, as well as lingering downgrade risks on its stock market.

Growth was supported by sectors such as manufacturing, including the processing of palm oil to produce fuel as Indonesia expanded its mandatory biodiesel programme, the statistics bureau said.

The 2026 state budget projects economic growth of 5.4 per cent, although finance minister Suahasil Nazara has said it could slightly exceed that target and reach 5.5 per cent this year.

The target falls within Bank Indonesia's GDP growth outlook range of 4.9 per cent to 5.7 per cent. At its meeting last month, the central bank said the domestic economy remained resilient but required further strengthening.

President Prabowo Subianto, who took office two years ago, aims to lift economic growth to 8 per cent by 2029.
